title: Modern Warfare 4 beta's first update is live, adding a new map, mode, and toned-down footsteps
author: Vikki Blake
content:
Infinity Ward has deployed the first proper update to the Modern Warfare 4 beta, addressing a chunk of the feedback from the beta's opening day, including footstep audio, weapon lethality, and map voting.
"We heard you loud and clear on the footstep volume, so we've adjusted things downward for today," the studio said in its official patch notes blog post. As a result, enemy footstep and gear audio have had both their volume and audible range reduced.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 | Multiplayer Trailer.Watch on YouTube
Time-to-kill has also been tuned down on some weapons, with the ISO Nightshade SMG and Oris 8.6 marksman rifle both seeing their damage ranges and headshot multipliers reduced.
Infinity Ward says these are just the first adjustments and more changes are coming as it continues reviewing feedback and data.
A new map, Cachette, and a new mode, Inflation, have also joined the multiplayer rotation. Inflation tasks players with eliminating enemies and defeating HVT operators to collect cash, with the richest players becoming marked targets for everyone else to hunt. Cachette's addition also means there are now enough maps in the pool for map voting to be switched on, something Infinity Ward said needed four total maps to work properly.
Elsewhere, Transit 213 has had its shadowed areas brightened and its overall colour balance adjusted for visibility, and there's a long list of smaller bug fixes, covering everything from Mobility Course completion issues to controller reconnection errors. On PC, Infinity Ward says it's working to improve the Secure Attestation Wizard, the tool used to diagnose and fix issues getting into the beta.
Not everything's fixed yet, though: join in progress remains temporarily disabled on Kill Block, and cooking certain lethals can still cause an FPS drop, both of which Infinity Ward says it's still working on.
Day 1 of the #MW4 Beta is almost in the books. We saw the conversation, and we're already cooking our first update for tomorrow with:
🔊 Footstep audio tuning 🗳️ Map voting turned on 🔫 Weapon balance adjustments 🛠️ Bug fixes and more
To see this content please enable targeting cookies.
Here's the full patch notes:
Thank you to everyone for your energy on Day 1 of the Early Access Beta. We had a blast playing with you, and we're ready to run it back all weekend.
Day 2 will bring a variety of bug fixes and gameplay adjustments, including a new Map and Mode which join the Multiplayer rotation at 10:00am PT
We'll be deploying an update shortly that aims to address a lot of the community feedback from yesterday. We heard you loud and clear on the footstep volume, so we've adjusted things downward for today. We've been following the conversation and agree that time-to-kill (TTK) isn't quite right yet, so we've tuned down the lethality of some of our guns to start. Finally, we made a tweak to boost visibility on Transit 213. Let us know if you think these adjustments are in the right direction, and expect more in the future.
We also know some of you had some trouble getting into the Beta yesterday, and we'll be working over time to clarify in-game error messaging and improve our Secure Attestation Wizard for PC players. Keep in mind the wizard doesn't just diagnose issues, it fixes them too, so give it a try if you haven't already.
We're working every day of the Beta to improve the experience, so keep the feedback coming. We're listening.
CONTENT
Maps
NEW: Cachette
Modes
NEW: Inflation
Eliminate enemies to collect cash.
Defeat HVT Operators to steal the cash they're carrying.
The richest players become marked HVTs for everyone to hunt.
Survive Overtime and get increased cash multipliers.
Here are the Patch Notes for today's update:
MAPS
Map Voting
We need 4 total maps to enable voting effectively, so with Cachette in the mix this is coming with today's update.
Transit 213
Brightened shadowed areas.
Adjusted overall color balance.
WEAPONS & ATTACHMENTS
An extra word from the Weapons Team:
Thanks for joining us in the Beta! The changes below are the ones we're already feeling good about, and we're keeping an eye on your feedback and data. Keep sharing it, we're listening!
Reduced the distance at which enemy footstep and gear audio can be heard.
Decreased overall enemy footstep and gear audio volume.
Our objective for movement audio is to indicate when enemies are approaching without revealing their exact positions at a distance. We'll continue looking at feedback on this topic throughout the Beta.
CHALLENGES
Daily Challenges
Enabled the ability to reroll Daily Challenges.
BUG FIXES
Fixed an issue where players were unable to start or complete the Mobility Course.
Fixed a bug that could cause footstep audio to incorrectly use wet-surface sounds when players were moving across dry areas.
Fixed an issue that prevented the Global Panel from being opened using its assigned keybind.
Fixed a disconnect issue caused by Seeker Drones.
Fixed various errors when navigating in the front-end menu.
Fixed an issue that could cause an error when entering the Gunsmith without a valid Weapon selected.
Fixed various errors when switching between or reconnecting controllers.
Fixed an issue where joining a friend from the menu would prevent you from being able to access some settings.
Fixed a bug that caused party members to remain in a looping animation in the Multiplayer Lobby.
Fixed an issue that could make certain magnified Optics opaque while aiming down sights.
Fixed a rare disconnect issue in Gunfight 10v10.
KNOWN ISSUES
Join in progress is temporarily disabled on Kill Block
We know this isn't ideal! We're actively working on a fix for this issue that's caused by a bug in the round transition.
Cooking some lethals can result in an FPS drop.
We're investigating reports of this and hope to have a fix soon.
We love seeing your posts, clips, and videos - keep them coming. Your feedback is what is going to make this game the best Modern Warfare, and we're focused on those improvements.
We'll see you in the lobby.
It follows a separate blog post from the developers earlier this week that addressed the beta's fix for "Compiling Shaders" stutter on PC, an issue common enough across the industry that it's notable when a game doesn't have it.
The first leg of the beta went live following the conclusion of Call of Duty: Next, the showcase event where many of the beta's maps and modes were revealed. This is Early Access, running until 25th August for anyone who's pre-ordered, ahead of a separate Open Beta weekend from 28th August to 1st September that's free for everyone.
summary: Infinity Ward has released the first update for the Modern Warfare 4 beta, addressing community feedback by lowering footstep volume and reducing weapon lethality. The patch also introduces a new map named Cachette and a new mode called Inflation, which enables map voting to be turned on. Additionally, the update features visibility improvements for the Transit 213 map and includes numerous bug fixes.
key_points: Enemy footstep and gear audio volume and range have been reduced based on player feedback.
Weapon lethality was adjusted, lowering damage ranges and headshot multipliers for the ISO Nightshade SMG and Oris 8.6 marksman rifle.
A new map, Cachette, and a new mode, Inflation, were added to the multiplayer rotation.
Map voting has been enabled now that four total maps are available in the pool.
Transit 213 received visibility updates with brightened shadowed areas and adjusted color balance.

title: Deals: Pixel 11 lineup goes on sale, latest Galaxy phones get discounts
author: Siddharth
content:
The Google Pixel 11 series, which went up for pre-order last week, is now officially available for purchase on Amazon UK. Alongside the Pixel phones, Samsung’s latest Galaxy foldables and the Galaxy S26 series have received price cuts.
While the Google Pixel 11 lineup hasn’t received any price cut, users are eligible for an added trade-in bonus when exchanging a compatible used phone. Customers will also receive £100 to purchase other Google products.
The new Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro/Pro XL, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold are now powered by a Tensor G6 chipset. The phones also get new color options, upgraded cameras, and other software improvements.
Next up, we’ve got Samsung’s latest Galaxy Z foldables, which can be £100 cheaper for Prime and Prime Student members. Customers will also get £50 off when they pair a Galaxy Watch9 or Watch Ultra2 with their purchase.
The Galaxy Z Fold8 introduces a brand-new wide form-factor in the Galaxy Z lineup with a cover screen that offers a 4:3 aspect ratio. Meanwhile, the Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra is the successor to last year’s Galaxy Z Fold7 and the Galaxy Z Flip8 offers minor upgrades that include a new chipset.
Alongside the foldables, Samsung’s current Galaxy S flagship series is also on sale. The Galaxy S26 and Galaxy S26+ have received a £100 discount, whereas the Galaxy S26 Ultra is £150 off its retail price.
The Galaxy S26 Ultra comes with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy chipset and a Privacy Display feature. Meanwhile, the standard Galaxy S26 and the Galaxy S26+ come equipped with an Exynos 2600 chipset.
Samsung’s Galaxy A57 is also on sale with a £100 discount on the 256GB variant. It comes with a 6.7-inch AMOLED display and a 5,000mAh battery.
The phone also offers a triple-rear camera setup with a 50MP main sensor and is powered by the Exynos 1680 SoC.
Lastly, we’ve got a couple of Oppo smartphones on discount, the Reno16 Pro and Reno16 to be exact.
The Pro variant is available with a £150 discount, whereas the standard Reno16 is £100 off its regular price.
The Reno16 Pro gets a 6.32-inch AMOLED display, a 6,700mAh battery, a 200MP main rear camera, and is powered by the Dimensity 8550 Super chipset. On the other hand, the Reno16 offers the same display and battery, but gets a 50MP main rear camera and is equipped with a Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 SoC.
We may get a commission from qualifying sales.
summary: The Google Pixel 11 series is now available on Amazon UK with trade-in bonuses and promotional credit, while various Samsung Galaxy and Oppo smartphones have received price cuts. Samsung's discounts cover its latest foldables, the Galaxy S26 flagship series, and the Galaxy A57. Additionally, Oppo's Reno16 Pro and Reno16 models are currently on sale with reduced prices.
key_points: The Google Pixel 11 lineup is officially on sale on Amazon UK, offering trade-in bonuses and £100 to spend on other Google products.
Samsung Galaxy Z foldables are £100 cheaper for Prime members, with an extra £50 off when paired with select Galaxy Watches.
The Galaxy S26 series features discounts ranging from £100 to £150 depending on the model.
The Samsung Galaxy A57 (256GB variant) and Oppo's Reno16 and Reno16 Pro are also available at discounted prices.

title: Call Of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Switch 2 Partner Developer Revealed By Activision
author: Nintendo Life; Liam Doolan
content:
![Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4](https://images.nintendolife.com/68eed6e64897d/call-of-duty-modern-warfare-4.900x.jpg)
Call of Duty is making its return to Nintendo platforms after 13 years this October, and Activision has revealed the developer who helped with the Switch 2 version of Modern Warfare 4.
Infinity Ward called on Activision's partners at Digital Legends. The Spanish-based studio, founded in 2001, made a name for itself as a mobile developer and was acquired by Activision in 2021. Since then, it's been assigned to multiple Call of Duty titles, including Black Ops 6, 7 and Warzone.
The studio has also shared an official announcement about its work on the native version of Modern Warfare 4 for Switch 2:
Digital Legends Entertainment: "Breaking boundaries once again! Infinity Ward, in partnership with Digital Legends, is developing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 natively for Nintendo Switch 2, bringing the MW series to Nintendo players for the first time in more than a decade. More to come later this summer!"
Activision has already given select creators and outlets an opportunity to go hands on with the Switch 2 version of Modern Warfare 4 ahead of next week's open beta, and the first impressions seem to be relatively positive.
The open beta for Switch 2 gets underway on 28th August 2026 and will include the campaign mission 'Entrenched' and multiplayer, including crossplay support. The full game arrives later this year on 23rd October 2026, with the Switch 2 version launching the same day as other platforms.
summary: Activision has revealed that Spanish-based developer Digital Legends is partnering with Infinity Ward to develop Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 natively for the Nintendo Switch 2. This release marks the franchise's return to Nintendo platforms after 13 years, launching on October 23, 2026. Ahead of the full launch, an open beta for the Switch 2 version featuring crossplay support is scheduled to begin on August 28, 2026.
key_points: Digital Legends is co-developing the native Nintendo Switch 2 version of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 with Infinity Ward.
The release marks the franchise's return to a Nintendo platform after a 13-year absence.
An open beta for the Switch 2 version featuring the campaign mission 'Entrenched' and crossplay multiplayer begins on August 28, 2026.
The full game is scheduled to launch on October 23, 2026, with the Switch 2 version releasing the same day as other platforms.

title: Double Fine's Tim Schafer confirms the studio now (almost) owns its own games again
author: Vikki Blake
content:
Double Fine has confirmed it owns – or will shortly own – the intellectual property and publishing rights to every game it made during its seven years under Xbox following the studio's split from Microsoft earlier this year.
CEO Tim Schafer confirmed the news on Kinda Funny Games (thanks, IGN), fielding a fan question about whether buying Double Fine's back catalogue - including Psychonauts 2, Keeper, and Kiln - actually puts money in the studio's pocket.
"I saw a question there: 'Do you guys make the money on games?'" Schafer said. "The transfer of the IP came back to us, and we get the publishing rights back to all our games."
That said, "some of [the games]" remain with Xbox for the time being, but Schafer explained that "it just takes a while for it to all process".
"If you're curious, buying any of our games helps support the studio," he emphasised. "We can turn that money into revenue that helps us extend that runway."
Schafer also revealed Double Fine's next move will be to revive its Amnesia Fortnight game jam as a Kickstarter campaign, letting backers vote on which prototype becomes the studio's next full project. The jam is set to run from 31st August through most of September.
It's the clearest confirmation yet of how Double Fine has come out the other side of Xbox's restructuring. Xbox's wider reorganisation, announced by CEO Asha Sharma in July, affected around 3,200 roles across the division and saw several studios, including Double Fine, spun back out into independence while keeping hold of their IP and back catalogues.
Double Fine itself laid off roughly a quarter of its 90-person team as part of the transition, saying at the time that the cuts were needed to reach "a size that we can sustain."
Compulsion Games, the We Happy Few and South of Midnight studio also cut loose from Xbox in the same restructuring, has similarly confirmed it retains ownership of its IP.
summary: Double Fine CEO Tim Schafer confirmed that the studio now owns or will soon own the intellectual property and publishing rights to all games made during its seven years under Xbox. Following the studio's independence resulting from Xbox restructuring, purchasing these games will directly support the studio's revenue. Additionally, Double Fine plans to revive its Amnesia Fortnight game jam through a Kickstarter campaign.
key_points: Double Fine regained intellectual property and publishing rights to its games following its split from Microsoft.
CEO Tim Schafer confirmed that buying Double Fine's back catalogue directly supports the studio's revenue.
The studio plans to launch a Kickstarter campaign for its Amnesia Fortnight game jam from August 31 through September.
The studio's return to independence followed a wider Xbox restructuring in July that affected multiple studios.

title: Camera AirPods Code Reveals Image Capture Resolution, Status Light, Person Detection, and More
author: Tim Hardwick
content:
Apple is working on camera-equipped AirPods, as indicated by various reports and a demo video of them in action discovered earlier this week. The video was found by MacRumors in the macOS Tahoe 26.7 release candidate, but it turns out there are even more details in the code.
![airpods pro 3 orange](https://images.macrumors.com/t/P5RFPWoCv1u8Rklkr3eIR7wYHcA=/400x0/article-new/2026/06/airpods-pro-3-orange.jpeg?lossy)
MacRumors forum member mactracker has discovered a hidden macOS framework called "AccessorySensorManager" that manages sensor data from the AirPods when they are connected to a Mac. That's turned up the following information:
- AirPods designed to capture paired color images: Code indicates the left and right earbuds have individual camera sensors that return synchronised RGB still images of up to 1 megapixel with matching frame IDs, giving Visual Intelligence the same scene from two angles. This doesn't rule out other sensors like infrared cameras, but they aren't mentioned in the code.
- AirPods support periodic image capture but not video: The cameras take internal still frames for Visual Intelligence to process, rather than "taking pictures" or recording video. In "active" mode, the framework can request a synced pair of images, or it can receive a capture rate, where pairs of stills are continually sent at the specified rate.
- Active and passive capture modes use different resolutions: In "active" mode, likely triggered by the user via Siri, the AirPods capture a 640x640 image and return a processed 1024x1024 image. "That's about 0.4 megapixels of sampled image data, and a little over 1 megapixel for the output frame," mactracker explains. In "passive" mode, they capture a 320x320 image that can return a 320×320 or 512×512 output. "These are capture-specific resolutions, and the physical sensor's native resolution may be larger," adds mactracker.
- Passive mode appears intended for background environmental awareness: The framework mentions contextual conditions like nearby speech, changes in the surrounding audio, posture changes, head rotation, and movement outside a defined area. It's not clear from the code whether every condition triggers a camera capture.
- AirPods account for continual head movement: The framework includes lens distortion correction, dual-camera calibration, and camera-to-motion sensor calibration. It can also reject images affected by excessive movement or an occluded view.
- Some processing happens directly on AirPods: The code mentions "peripheral inference," or on-device detection of whether a person is in view.
- Each AirPod likely has a capture indicator light: The framework contains code that allows it to remotely control a hardware indicator and its brightness, suggesting the AirPods have a light to let other people know when they are capturing still images.
It's worth noting that the AirPods that were shown in the demo video were a version of the AirPods Pro 3 with cameras, which have a B790 codename. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman has said that Apple no longer plans to release this model, and instead is working on a new generation of AirPods with cameras, codenamed B798. This makes it likely that the discovered framework is related to the canceled model. It also underlines that the findings show how Apple's camera-equipped AirPods could work, rather than a guarantee of the final product's features.
Gurman says the AirPods are planned for 2027, and could potentially launch alongside the 20th-anniversary iPhone.
summary: Apple code discovered in a macOS release candidate reveals details about camera-equipped AirPods designed to capture synchronized RGB still images for Visual Intelligence. The framework outlines active and passive capture modes, on-device person detection, and a hardware indicator light for privacy. While the code suggests how these features could function, reports indicate the specific tested prototype was canceled in favor of a newer generation planned for 2027.
key_points: Left and right earbuds contain individual camera sensors that capture synchronized RGB still images up to 1 megapixel.
The framework supports both an active mode for user-triggered captures and a passive mode intended for background environmental awareness.
Code references peripheral inference to detect whether a person is in view directly on the device.
A hardware indicator light with adjustable brightness appears designed to signal when images are being captured.
The discovered code is likely tied to a canceled AirPods Pro 3 prototype codenamed B790, with a new generation expected around 2027.

title: ‘GTA 6’ Leaker Has Now Reached A Strip Club As Rockstar Scrambles
author: Paul Tassi
content:
The Grand Theft Auto 6 leaker is alive and well, as a new report yesterday indicates that Take-Two and Rockstar still do not know who is behind the leak nor how it happened in the first place. The publisher is now subpoenaing Microsoft and Discord to try to get information to track the leaker down, but here on Saturday morning, the 7th footage release from Cyberleek is live. And things are certainly progressing.
The new clip has more typical Grand Theft Auto tomfoolery, showing in GTA 6 you can, of course, rob stores. Here, Jason robs two gas stations as the police ramp up pursuit. At one point, he gets into a car crash so severe the camera shifts into slow motion.
However, the end of the clip shows Jason walking through the doors of a strip club, ending the video before anything inside is really seen. And, if you were paying attention, you would have seen a “$3 million market cap = strip club” watermark on all the just-released footage. This references what Cyberleek has been hawking this entire time, a meme coin meant to enrich the leaker over the course of this saga. They have also run paid polls on their site about what should be released next. They are not exactly painting a picture of themselves as a freedom fighter striking against the erasure of physical discs at this point.
Strip clubs in Grand Theft Auto games are sort of sacrosanct institutions for players, where decades ago, players could hardly believe something so scandalous could exist in a mainstream game. While not quite as revolutionary these days, millions of players are certainly curious to see what a GTA 6 strip club will look like in-game and just how MA-rated it may get. Unlike most of the other footage, it is almost certainly something that is not going to be shown in next week’s Netflix gameplay special.
![frase](https://images.forbes.com/fbs-games-assets/frase.png)
FEATURED | Frase ByForbes™
Unscramble The Anagram To Reveal The Phrase
![pinpoint](https://images.forbes.com/fbs-games-assets/pinpoint.png)
Pinpoint By Linkedin
Guess The Category
![queens](https://images.forbes.com/fbs-games-assets/queens.png)
Queens By Linkedin
Crown Each Region
![crossclimb](https://images.forbes.com/fbs-games-assets/crossclimb.png)
Crossclimb By Linkedin
Unlock A Trivia Ladder
As for this idea of pumping up his crypto coin to a $3 million market cap, as it stands, the coin seems to be at $1.5 million, so it would need to double. In 24 hours, the trading volume has been $1.4 million, meaning as scammy as this all seems, the audience is clearly interacting with it as these leaks rack up millions upon millions of views, multiplying even after takedown attempts. The risk of a potential rug pull here is blindingly obvious.
The biggest threat to GTA 6 right now remains story spoilers, something these leaks have avoided so far, but obviously Rockstar wants absolutely none of this out there. The strip club, as silly as it may sound, is a big deal to leak for the GTA 6 playerbase. That may be next, it may not, but that’s the point, no one, including Rockstar and Take-Two, knows what’s going to show up with each new drop.
Follow me on Twitter, YouTube, and Instagram.
Pick up my sci-fi novels the Herokiller series and The Earthborn Trilogy.
summary: Take-Two and Rockstar have yet to identify the person behind the Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks as a new seventh video clip is released. The latest footage shows gameplay elements like store robberies and ends at the entrance of a strip club. Meanwhile, the leaker continues to promote a meme coin tied to the release of the footage.
key_points: Publisher Take-Two and Rockstar still do not know who is responsible for the leaks or how they happened.
The newest leaked footage shows a character named Jason robbing gas stations and approaching a strip club.
The leaker is promoting a meme coin linked to the release of the leaked videos.
Despite takedown attempts, the leaks continue to rack up millions of views.

title: Raphaël Colantonio interview: What it would take to make Dishonored 3, where Grand Theft Auto VI could fall short, and what's next for the founder of Arkane Studios | Press Box PR
author: Greg Johnson
content:
In an exclusive interview with Press Box PR, Arkane Studios founder Raphaël Colantonio has spoken about what fans can expect from his next project, the reasons why there isn't a third Dishonored game on the release schedule, and what he would create if Rockstar asked him to lead the development of a future Grand Theft Auto game.
The French video game design legend, now Creative Director of WolfEye Studios, also gave his thoughts on the costs of games today, what it was like to work for Valve and how he and his team like to approach game development as an artform.
Read the full interview below.
How proud of you are you of Dishonoured and the world you and your team built that people are engrossed in today, so many years later?
It is beyond what we could have imagined.
When I started to make video games, my hope was that I would make games that somehow had that same impact on people as the games that I loved back then when I was a kid, you know? 
Part of me believed it was possible. The other part of me thought it would be incredible if it could ever happen. We all have different voices in our heads and there’s that hope but also the more realistic version that is going to say, come on now, who do you think you are or whatever. 
And the truth is, yes, it is incredible. And the truth is it's partially random. You know, when you reach something like that, it's a mix of being with the right people, because first of all, it was not just me. Harvey Smith, of course, was involved. Victor Antonov was incredible. Sébastien Mitton, Christophe Carrier, and Julien Roby, all the people that we had worked with for a long time, that eventually we grew together. 
We have that same passion together and it put us together in this same bag where all of us, absolutely all of us, were animated by the same values, the same passion, the same desire to make something with integrity and that we loved. And hoping or having the arrogance or the naivety that people would click with it.
But I can tell you, as we were making it, I remember, and I will always remember, we were in a meeting one day and Victor had so much self-confidence. He was that guy, right? And he said, with his really cool voice something like: ‘there was Dark City, there was Star Wars, and now there is Dunwall.’ We looked at each other and we were like, okay, that’s the spirit, and he was kind of right!
We were set to go for Game of the Year and I did announce that to the team at some point. I think maybe during beta. I told them, guys we are going for Game of the Year, and Arkane was not a team where people would be cynical and laugh things off but they reacted the same as I did with Victor. Wow, well if you think so! Hopefully, anyway. But you need that mix of being with the right people with the talent, hard work and luck to some degree.
We had Bethesda too, of course, and that’s the context where you look at all the ingredients to make such a fantastic game, something that hits like that, and even then the market needs to be ready for it. The inspiration needs to be there. You need a dream. You need the energy. And the publisher needs to give you all the means to do it, understand what you’re doing, and trust you, because frankly Dishonoured sucked until it was good.
The world was bizarre. I remember Harvey and I were constantly worried. Would any other people even give a shit about this world we were building? It was so strange. British-inspired but with some sorcery and at that point that was not a story that anyone could relate to. Really, who would even care? Of course, we made it, but we had that fear all along. We did everything we could to make sure that people would care more and more about things in the world. They would care about Emily, the little girl. We would make a few of the characters kind of vulnerable and nice so that you want to care for them. But when you don't know the end of the movie, when you don't know whether people are going to connect with what you’re making, trust me, you really are doing things from a place of doubt and fear. Eventually you let the fear and the doubt go and just go with what you love because that's really what it was all about all along. 
Again, I think the fact that it was a game made with integrity by a team of people who were working together for so long and shared the same values, and were assisted or at least empowered by a publisher that trusted us in spite of the delays, in spite of the game sucking for so long. And then with a marketing team that actually understood the game, put the money behind it. We had those giant billboards in New York and we hit it out of the park but you always feel like there were 10 targets to sit at a thousand yards. All of them had our snipers on them and there was some wind and everything else but we hit all of them. Including the lucky one.
For games as an industry to continue to grow, do we need more developers going on a journey to create something meaningful as you did rather than sticking to tried and tested formulas and repeating what they know works and makes money?
I mean, there are many forces against that. We can talk about AI, we can talk about the business mind in general. The business mind is always trying to find a formula. The business mind wants to replicate success. The business mind goes against art, goes against the magic, the luck, the effort and the unpredictability.
The business mind never really existed in the past in gaming but it’s as acute as it can be right now. Everyone wants growth. Everything wants to win. It is a hustling mentality. People don't want to make three times their money. They want to make 100 times more. They want to make 1,000 times more. People are in a hurry to be very rich and do anything to get there.
We’re in a weird world where the traditional gaming industry is now seen as the past and almost in a way too risky because yet again we are back to this question of what makes something a success? And for my part, and the part of the people that work with me now at Wolf-Eye, and that’s a lot of the same people that I've been working with for 30 years, we try to ignore it. 
I mean, it's impossible to ignore it entirely because we live in that world. So of course, when we look for a deal, when we deal with publishers, we have to deal with that. And when we open Twitter, we see the anger, the cynicism. We see all that. And it affects us to some degree. But at the end of the day, we can only control what we can control.
We're still animated by the same force. Why are we making games? We're not looking for a formula. There is no formula. Spoiler alert, sorry to disappoint, there's really no formula. Every time we struggle. Every time we're not sure what we're doing. We make tons of mistakes. We course correct while we're doing it. What is at stake is so big because the budgets are bigger and bigger so of course that it can be terrifying. 
On the one hand, I’m still that kid, I’m recruiting my inner kid, to make this baby that I know some players want to see because they want to see that passion, you know. When I was younger and I was playing games when I was 15 years old or something, there was nothing that possessed me more than video games. Maybe music was to the same level. 
I hope those games still exist. Occasionally I am touched by a game like that but it’s rare, and it’s because we are in a world, governed by money and easy tricks and shortcuts, how can we make more with less, how can you deliver, how can we milk the players and this and that. But my mindset, and the mindset of the people that I work with is still the same, I would say it is even the same since back in the days of Arx Fatalis, and that’s why we are making games. There’s no other reason. If there were any other reasons, all of us would be much more rich, but that is not what we pursue. 
What we pursue is to make another Dishonoured. When you make a game with integrity and it’s a hit, it’s totally validating, and not only validating of your work but also validating in what you believe in. You could read this as OK this guy wants some validation for his creativity or whatever but no, it’s about believing in doing things for the right reasons. We believe in making the games we do because there is a burning desire from the people making it to make this game see the day and connect with people. Not because it looks good on an Excel spreadsheet tracking the bottom line or whatever. That’s not where we come at it from. That will never be where our work comes from.
Is it harder to pitch the concept of open world to gamers now given how many games haven’t come through on the promise of the concept now that it has become a trend?
You know we’ve never followed trends. Of course, we adapt and we evolve because our own tastes evolve and adapt, and there are benefits to open world. There is something that feels more contiguous. In fact, if you look at Prey, Prey was contiguous. It was not mission based anymore. It was one big mission or several big missions that were intertwined in a big space where you could always backtrack and come back to and I think for this next game, that's something that we have in mind. It’s a little more of what we want, actually, and I would say for us, because we're not trying to chase a trend, we still want everything to feel very handcrafted. 
For us, we are delivering an extremely handcrafted open world. There's nothing set to random. There's nothing procedural about it. Of course that means it’s going to be smaller than other open worlds but at the same time, because as much as we follow our passion and our integrity, we are also always full of fears, right? So we always double check that we're not being stupid because everybody goes with giant open worlds these days. 
Thankfully, we realised how the majority of gamers are fed up with these grindy giant open world games where the metric of value is size and the trade off is that everything is shallow or repetitive. There's nothing that feels that it has meaning. There's no feel at all. So we accidentally, I guess, are more in line with the market because it's going to be a very handcrafted open world. You can go everywhere and everything you see you can go to. We don't cheat the player with fake environments. Nothing is generated on the fly in a procedural way. It's the good old style, created by hand, where everything has a meaning and has its place. 
So when exploring it, we want to make sure that people feel like everything is cohesive. Everything. That's the trade-off of small open worlds.
Is there a specific mechanic or signature element from your previous work as a team that you hope to explore even more deeply in your new game?
I wouldn’t even know at this point. There are so many people that come from the same DNA that we undoubtedly do things in a very similar way as we always have done so a lot of the feeling that people have had before, they will find it again.
You know, we started out with those filters. We wanted to create a game like Fallout meets Dishonoured or something, or a game in keeping with Arkane Games to be more accurate, specifically Dishonoured. So what we want is to land in the Action RPG space with all those values, dialogue and so on, and that’s still our inspiration.
I think where we will eventually land is, well, the game will land where it lands. It’s not going to be this perfect, absolutely exact percentage of this game or that because every time we have made a game, even when we made Dishonoured, we started to show it to the press and the press were always saying the same thing. It was interesting. They said it was Bioshock meets Assassin’s Creed and I can guarantee you that today, if you were asking the press to describe Dishonored, they probably would not say it's Bioshock meets Assassin's Creed. 
I mean, I love Bioshock and yes, we were playing as an assassin, so they are not bad references to pull from. It wasn’t insulting in any way. It did just make us feel like… why are you pigeonholing us? It’s not this meets that but instead it was its own thing. If we wanted to be more accurate, we cold have said it was like Thief on steroids in an interesting world, not that Thief’s world wasn’t interesting in its own right. I think Dishonoured was like a secret handshake for Thief fans.
But what is this new game going to be? I don’t want to describe it exactly, only because it’s too early and I want us to be ready before really talk about the game, but of course our values are our values and it has a lot of the same people behind it. That’s unavoidable and there’s going to be a lot of things where if you watch 10 films from the same team you will probably have some consistency in taste and flavour even if each film might be different.
How have you been finding the early play testing sessions and how important is testing with external players to get the game feeling and playing right?
Testing with people from outside of the team is very, very interesting. It’s an interesting topic in general because you don’t want to make a game by numbers or even by theory because you risk making something formulaic. But at the same time, you don’t want to make something totally in a vacuum where it doesn’t hit what people want at all.
In the past, when we were making Dishonored or Prey, I would say for those two games, we would of course use testers we were familiar with and it’s pretty similar this time around. So far we haven't opened it to the public. We've looked at tiers. So far we've invited the players that played Weird West before. We've invited the people that we really trusted, first of all, so that they would not share anything outside of the company. When you go to the next round of going to the public it might be more risky where some things will leak things and we absolutely didn't want anything to leak. 
Also, with the game being in progress for so long, when you make a game, most of the time is about assembling things together without necessarily having too much of a game to play so that requires a specific type of tester. You need people who are able to hold their breath and imagine beyond what they currently see. That’s hard.
These people are typically also very, very critical. They’re very smart. They're very competent. Great, great gamers. They will just tell you what they think and you cannot ignore it.
However, you cannot be too paralysed by it either because often people will say something with very cutting words and that has value, right? Then it's up to you what you do with it. You can look at it the way we look at the trends. Unfortunately, sometimes, you can have something that is not really a trend and it is extremely polarising but like, man, that was the best part of the game. Then some other tester would say that what they hated the most was that same thing that this other guy liked. We've seen that. There's a few mechanics like that. And so it's one tool amongst others, feedback from people that you trust, from people that are smart. But smart people can say the wrong things too. Not everybody is right all the time.
Is there an inflection point where the value of taking your testing to the wider public becomes greater than the risk of leaks?
The truth is that different companies have different results with that approach.
There are some approaches that are super interesting. We haven't really gone to that point but there's a company I know who almost does the equivalent of crowdfunding but for design. They do crowd design. I don't think we could do that. 
That would be exhausting because it requires a different type of management. You could have, therefore, maybe 500 people or a thousand people that test the thing, give their feedback, then they do polling and votes. Every creative team has different things that they're comfortable with. That would be too much for me and I think for my team in general. 
For us, we've realised that most of the time, if you rotate your testers, that's more the Valve way of doing it, and that's more something we learned with Valve back in the day when we working for them on some stuff. You rotate people, and then the next set of people, and it can be five or 10 people at a time. Five then 10 then five then 10 and no matter what you realise that somehow this is enough to discover things.
The thing that we realised is if someone tests a level and they are a little lost, that's OK. But if you have five people that are lost out of 10, then already you have a problem. It means that, okay, put a light there. There's something that is missing in the direction.
Then the next time you test, now you have nobody getting lost and you go, that's it, we addressed it, because at this point you can guarantee that you're probably fine. It’s very likely that if you have a significant number of testers, you don’t need a thousand, you might just need a hundred. You don’t need 10,000. You don’t need a million.
If you have 100 testers, you’re probably going to have the same results as 1,000 testers. The difference is that with 1,000 testers, you might want to use that as marketing because that can create momentum by having early advocates for your game. I think that’s part of the early access strategy. People don’t only offer early access because they want to test the market. Yes, it’s going to give you a lot of bug testers so there’s a value there but by offering early access you now also have 10,000 or 50,000 people that are invested in your game. They're going to talk about your game to all their friends. 
You also find yourself at greater risk of leaks so if you do that, you do it as late as possible. Look at Baldur’s Gate 3. They did that. For them, it was fantastic because that game is so systematic and there are so many possibilities that testing it out with a hundred testers would have been impossible. In their case, it made sense to have thousands of testers. I don’t know how late they went into that process. I think the strategy was to do it as early as possible once the game was already fun, and then they opened up the first chapter or something. There's a lot of interesting decisions they made about that. That was very smart. They had the best of both worlds because even if it leaked, they could not leak the entire game. 
There's a lot of things I could say here about our plans but I don't know where we stand. We're definitely going to open it up to a bigger portion of players at some point, and probably bigger than we've ever opened it before because we too have a game with tons and tons of possibilities and there will be a moment where having a lot of testing is going to help us. But it's not really my side, so I might say the wrong things here and I don’t want to take the risk.
Would you still be interested in going back to do Dishonoured 3? What are the stories still to be told in that world?
You know, it's funny because I think I've had my version of what could become Dishonoured 3. Harvey Smith has had his version. Ricardo Bare has had his version too. None of them are all the same at all.
I don't know where we would all take it for a third game because we definitely closed the story of Emily and Corvo in the second game so it would have to be something else. It could be more like a sequel where you try to take on the whole world. Then the spirit of the player experience, what to do in the game, what other things you can do, it would be an interesting thing.
In an alternate dimension, I'm sure it would be great for Harvey, myself, Ricardo, Dinga Bakaba and Sébastien Mitton to be reunited and put Christophe Carrier in there and make it but we only have one life so it would probably never happen. But it would be an interesting thing to create.
Given your upcoming game and the new game from Harvey, Dishonoured fans may be getting two spiritual sequels even if they won’t get a direct sequel?
Yes, that's another way to look at it.
I think with some properties, I understand there could be more stuff to say about the world of Dishonoured, but you need someone behind it that really wants to make it. It cannot just be because it would be a nice number to have. It’s got to be something we want to do that I think we do something great with.
We have to commit five years of our lives to creating a game because that’s what it takes now. If you include all the pre-thinking, the meetings, the production, the post-production, being late, it always takes forever to make a game. 
If Rockstar tapped you on the shoulder and said Raf, we want you to come in to lead the creation of GTA 7 to fit your vision, your philosophy, your ideas, your values, what would that game look like?
I could get myself in trouble by talking about Grand Theft Auto because I think they are the biggest tease and at the same time the biggest disappointment when you love immersive sims. 
I don't mean that in an offensive way because of course who am I and who are they? They make games that sell I don't know how many thousands times more than mine and they are so incredible at doing surface simulation. But that’s such a stab in the heart for me when they don’t go more than surface level where there’s no long-term consequences to anything you do. 
It's more like a fantastic sandbox with incredible execution, incredible cinematography, great gameplay and you know they score — bam, bam, bam — nonstop because they deliver a player experience people connect with, you know, gangsters in LA and that kind of thing.
They’ve got that down and I understand why they do it, and by the way, a lot of this is probably a legacy of them having started this formula in the nineties, the same way that Resident Evil follows a formula to some degree. I suspect they still have those typewriters in the basement to set you a scheme. I don't know if they do that but it was always funny to me. It's possible that GTA have their version of that, which is the fact that they open an instance of the world for a mission that changes absolutely everything, both for them and both for us.
If you think of Skyrim, there's no instance of anything. There's just one instance of the world. You play the game and then things start to bleed onto each other and then it's a mess and now you have this town and when you come back you have to sneak around to do something because the guards would chase you down. You really own your consequences as a player. Everything is playable and you have to deal with your choices for the rest of the game. 
What Rockstar basically say is, you know what? That part sucks. It’s too hard to do. It confuses players and most players won’t care at all anyway. Here’s what we will do instead. We put a guy with a question mark on their head. They have a mission for you. When you want to play the mission, we open an instance of the world in which nothing else matters than what's inside this instance. Then, because of that there is a trade off. 
The positive is that we can do whatever we want. We can do all the crazy things with the cops coming in, the building exploding, everything we want. People are going to be thrilled but none of it matters. That's the thing. We don't have to deal with the consequences. The players don't have to deal with the consequences. Therefore, we can push the buttons, crank things up to 11, and I totally get the draw. 
I totally understand why people are into it. I understand why they would be into it as developers. I understand why it sells so much but this is not my values, not that my values are not to sell a gazillion units! But my values are not to pause the simulation for an instance to then resume the world later. What happens in those games is that if you do something wrong that leads to a mission failure. That doesn't exist in our games. We don't have the concepts of failures.
If you fail the mission, you find yourself back out on the street and there’s the same guy with the same question mark over his head who you click on and you’re ready to restart the mission. There’s nothing immersive to me in that.
I'm trying to say this with the greatest respect for them because I do respect them. What they do, I could not do. They do things that are amazing and I can already imagine the public flaming of what I am saying because that's how the world is nowadays. But no, I respect them a lot. It's just that it's not my bike.
What if Rockstar wanted to make an immersive sim with their next GTA game?
I’d say guys, you don't want to always boost your sales. You want to lower the sales. No, I think they know what they do very, very well. It's highly respectable. It's great in so many ways. It's just not my thing, and I couldn't imagine a world where they would want me in there because I'm going to bring some bizarre stuff. They're going for more direct paraphernalia where instantly
you know the gameplay. It doesn't need digestion and there isn’t anything obscure like what we do here, so yeah it's a difference like the difference between Steven Spielberg and David Lynch or whatever. One is going to sell gazillions and the other one is going to be a little more indirect and obscure and sometimes land a hit. I don't know, maybe that was a weird comparison but like everybody else I'm really, really looking forward to GTA VI mostly because I want to see how far they can push the instant simulation, surface simulation, because they do all that so incredibly well, and it's inspiring, and I love that.
What can you tell me about the project you worked on with Valve around a game set around Ravenholm?
It took us a decade to move on from the pain of the Ravenholm project because we were incredibly excited about doing that game and we put in a lot of creative energy into it and eventually when the decision was made to cut it, we did not understand it as it happened.
We were young and we were just refusing to see the reality of the situation and the reality was much simpler than the way it looked to us. It all came down to the economics behind Half Life 2 and how the DLCs were selling. They had a business ratio between how much they could spend and how they could make it to be worth it to them because it takes the attention of the entire structure on their side.
They had tried to create something internally and then they had tried with an external team already in America but it did not work out because they were too expensive so they worked with us because they liked our work and we worked with them during that time. They thought, you know, why not try these guys? We seemed pretty effective and eventually, like the two other attempts that they had looked at, we went somewhere with it, and it was cool. What we had was really, really cool. But it still needed more time, and too much time to finish. Beyond it being cool there was a business call at some point where it was decided that it didn’t really make sense. It was very painful for us but it made sense, we grew up and got a little bit more mature about it.
It also led us to work very closely with Viktor Antonov and eventually he joined us to create Dishonoured and we did not betray the Valve mentality. We learned a lot from them, actually. It’s just that we probably snuck in some of our own Arkane stuff in there as well. It had everything you would expect with little gadgets that are maybe a little bit more indirect, and maybe there was a little bit more verticality in some ways with the mobility, because that’s always something that we’ve been obsessed with. 
But how would I like to see them play it with Half Life 3? You know, I wouldn't have the arrogance to say anything about that. I think they are the grand masters. We've learned from them. We admired them. We still admire them. The bar is so high but I have no doubt that they will rise to meet it because I want to play a fantastic Half Life 3. I just trust that they have the time to do it right.
Is there another IP you and your team would like to work on some day?
Now that we're working on a new IP, that's probably the IP we want to work on. 
I think an IP is a love story between the creator and the IP and I think that's the thing we love at the moment. 
As much as I've really, really loved doing Arx Fatalis, for example, I don't know if I would come back to it now because if I was to work on these things in parallel, it would be a different thing. The way I work right now is that I put in my entire time and it’s the same for my team. We're all exclusive in a way. So then you think, well, I'm gonna spend another four or five years of my life on this, or three years because if it's a sequel, it's probably less. It’s got to be something that actually matters to you so I think right now my dream game would be this current IP that I'm working on.
What’s your view on the great debate over $100 games?
I don't know if it’s because I'm an old gamer but I remember when games actually were priced at $100. 
Back when I was 15 years old a game in France would cost 500 francs which was just shy of $100. We're talking about 1985 or 1990 so the equivalent in real terms in modern money would be much more than that, probably three times that. It would be like spending $300 on a game. But the habits were different back then. People would invest in the game. Those were the days where you would think of the game that you want to buy, maybe you only buy five per year, and this is going to cost you the equivalent of $300 each time.
So when I hear about games costing $100, on one hand I think it's outrageous and on the other hand it's like, whatever. I’d $100 for the next Baldur's Gate. For me it's all about how much I love it because if it's going hold me for a month as a player,
Think about it this way. You’d spend $100 for dinner at some steakhouse with some wine and the next day it’s gone. You spend $100 on a game, you put it down for the night, and it’s still there the next day. I don’t know, everything is relative I guess.
I don't necessarily understand why it's going up. In the sense that the markets should be expanding. We should be selling more units than we were selling in the 80s so it should be the opposite, if anything. Games should be getting cheaper. The cost of games should go down. But for some reason they're going to those higher prices.
But that’s not my area. I make games. I want them to be priced right. I think our game will be priced right because I trust the publisher that we work with.
I don't understand why they go up but if they do go up, it's not the end of the world as long as we still get good games. What's more worrying for me is that there are less and less games that I'm excited about.
summary: In an exclusive interview, Arkane Studios founder Raphaël Colantonio discussed the creation and legacy of Dishonored, reflecting on the doubt, collaboration, and publisher trust required to build its unique world. He also shared insights on game development as an art form, contrasting creative integrity against industry trends driven purely by financial formulas and massive budgets. Additionally, Colantonio explained that his team at WolfEye Studios focuses on crafting smaller, highly detailed, and non-procedural open worlds.
key_points: Dishonored was created through a mix of shared passion, a talented team, and a trusting publisher, despite initial doubts about whether players would connect with the strange world.
Colantonio criticizes the modern gaming industry's focus on business metrics, growth formulas, and easy shortcuts over artistic magic and integrity.
WolfEye Studios' upcoming game aims to feature a handcrafted, non-procedural open world where everything has meaning rather than relying on giant, repetitive environments.
The development process at WolfEye is guided by the same core values used during past projects like Dishonored, focusing on the action RPG space and meaningful player connections.

title: ‘It brings me joy’: how young people are making CDs cool again
author: Lauren Cochrane
content:
With more than 800 million people subscribing to a music streaming service, wireless speakers have become a familiar sight in homes. But expect to get reacquainted with a different object to play music soon: the CD player, once consigned to obsolescence, is back.
John Lewis report that searches for CD players are up 96% since July, possibly owing to students heading to university and buying the systems for their rooms. The £79 Crosley Voyager, and the £129 Pure Classic C-D6 are both sold out online, with the Voyager scheduled to return in October. Portable CD players are also popular.
This tallies, of course, with sales of CDs themselves. A report this year found that the growth of CD sales is up 16%, compared with vinyl’s 2.4%. HMV reports that sales of CDs are up 10% year on year – thanks to artists often providing unique content on the format. “K-pop has been a massive driver, with BTS the most obvious example of artists that have led the resurgence,” says the managing director, Phil Halliday. “But it goes much wider than that. We’re seeing very strong CD demand around artists like Olivia Rodrigo, Ariana Grande and Olivia Dean.”
![Woman browsing shelves of CDs](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1ab3fbd32d924c96f88757ee3caa42508e36c59e/0_0_5505_4404/master/5505.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The fact that a vinyl record is about £35, compared with £12 for a CD, is no doubt a factor.
Tom Morgan-Freelander, the deputy editor of the technology magazine Stuff, has noticed the change over the past two years. He puts it down to consumers wanting to move away from using their phone, a better audio quality, and limited disposable income. “It’s: ‘I don’t want to spend money on a turntable and the speakers that go with it. I want to spend £150 on an all-in-one system that comes with the CD player,’” he says.
In the CD aisle of an HMV in London on a weekday morning, people in their teens and twenties are browsing. Fourteen-year-old Milo Georgeaux-Healy has chosen two Dua Lipa albums as well as Brat by Charli xcx to play on an “old boombox”. “I like them because they’re cheaper,” she says. “They’re a lot more compact [than vinyl], and I find that they have better quality than your phone.” Adel Alsehi, 27, is visiting from Riyadh. He has selected a Madonna greatest hits, a Kacey Musgraves album and Private Dancer by Tina Turner. “It gives me a different feeling,” he says of CDs. “I feel like I’m listening to an artist’s work. It brings me joy.”
![Crosley Voyager CD player](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/8b031cad4c1bffe3f790239607a8f07aa76ab5ed/0_221_1440_1152/master/1440.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Richard Farnell runs Vinyl Exchange in Manchester, where they also sell CDs. He says the people buying CDs are now younger, and cost is a big part of this. “The record labels started to up the price of vinyl and it became largely unaffordable for this demographic,” he says. “A copy of Oasis’s Definitely Maybe on original UK “Damont” pressing can sell for between £150 and £250, depending upon condition. The standard vinyl reissue will be around £25-£30, but in our shop the CD version will only be £4.”
after newsletter promotion
The CD revival is part of a wider fashion for retro tech. As well as the vinyl resurgence and cassettes becoming popular items to buy, there’s the vogue for wearing wired earphones over AirPods. “The vinyl revival re-established our appetite for analogue, and now we’re seeing that broader love for physical music drive a genuine surge in CD players,” confirms Katrina Mills, the category buying lead for audio and imaging at John Lewis.
Part of this is about optics. “Someone walking around with a portable CD player and wired headphones is signalling their sense of taste and cultural capital,” says brand strategist Alexi Gunner. He has labelled this trend “performative audiophilia”.
Gunner argues that the return to the physical for music is a kind of rebellion. “The status quo is streaming platforms and wireless audio on identical iPhones,” he says. “All this has taken away the haptic, sensorial quality of listening to music.”
![A pile of CDs showing some of the main groups behind the 90s Britpop movement, including Blur, Oasis, Space, Kula Shaker, Suede and Supergrass](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/0be85309cbbf2c92e683a6de879ff71900152edf/0_0_5000_4000/master/5000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
J’Nae Phillips, who writes about Gen Z trends on her Substack Fashion Tingz, agrees. “When music is effectively infinite and frictionless, something is appealing about having to choose an album, put a disc in and listen to it from beginning to end,” she says, and echoes Gunner’s point: “There’s a certain cultural cachet in showing that you’re interested in music as an object and an experience, rather than simply consuming whatever happens to be recommended by an algorithm.”
Arguably, the CD is the final revival available to young people – it’s the last format for music before the MP3 arrived in the early 2000s. However, Gunner suggests there may be a different object waiting in the wings: the USB stick. Fred Again named his 2025 tour after the portable drive. “It’s the most common format that a DJ will carry their music to a gig on,” explains Gunner. “In the frame of performative audiophilia, you’re showing that you’re not just listening to music, you are possibly a DJ, you are a tastemaker … it’s something that will become more popular.”
summary: CDs and CD players are experiencing a resurgence in popularity, particularly among young people and university students. Driven by factors such as affordability compared to vinyl, a desire for better audio quality, and a rejection of phone-based streaming, consumers are embracing physical media as a form of retro culture and tactile engagement. Retailers like John Lewis and HMV report significant increases in searches and sales for both players and discs.
key_points: John Lewis reports a 96% increase in searches for CD players since July.
CD sales have grown by 16%, outpacing the growth rate of vinyl records.
K-pop acts like BTS, along with Western artists like Olivia Rodrigo and Charli xcx, are major drivers of CD demand.
CDs are significantly cheaper than vinyl, making them more accessible for younger consumers with limited disposable income.
Experts attribute the trend to consumers wanting to move away from phones, streaming algorithms, and wireless audio in favor of physical, intentional music experiences.

title: Apple Reportedly Lays Off 60 Vision Products Group Employees
author: Tim Hardwick
content:
Apple "has just laid off an entire team dedicated to VR development," reports AppleInsider, citing its own source. Apple is said to have laid off at least 60 employees from its Apple Vision Group.
![Apple Vision Pro Dual Knit Band](https://images.macrumors.com/t/5DQwPPOl9Eopsx8eKkN34cgMiSk=/400x0/article-new/2025/10/Apple-Vision-Pro-Dual-Knit-Band.jpg?lossy)
Bloomberg's Mark Gurman previously reported that the Vision Pro team was disbanded and its members redistributed across other projects, following the October 2025 refresh of the Vision Pro and the headset's weak reception. 
Incoming Apple CEO John Ternus also reportedly signed off on canceling both a second Vision Pro and a cheaper, slimmer "Vision Air," with Apple's focus now shifted to smart glasses.
Last month, The Elec reported that Apple had suspended development of the display for a cheaper, lighter version of the Vision Pro that it originally planned to launch in the next few years. Gurman doesn't expect Apple to launch another headset before late 2028 at the earliest.
summary: Apple has reportedly laid off at least 60 employees from its Apple Vision Group and disbanded a team dedicated to VR development. Following the weak reception of the Vision Pro, incoming CEO John Ternus allegedly canceled plans for a second-generation Vision Pro and a cheaper 'Vision Air' model. Apple has shifted its hardware focus toward smart glasses, and a new headset is not expected until at least late 2028.
key_points: Apple laid off at least 60 employees from its Apple Vision Group.
A team dedicated to VR development was disbanded following weak reception of the Vision Pro.
Plans for a second Vision Pro and a cheaper 'Vision Air' were reportedly canceled by incoming CEO John Ternus.
Apple has shifted its primary focus to smart glasses development.
A new headset is not anticipated to launch before late 2028 at the earliest.

title: It's Time. How to Get Early Access to the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Beta
author: Jason Cohen
content:
![](https://sm.pcmag.com/t/pcmag_uk/news/i/its-time-h/its-time-how-to-get-early-access-to-the-call-of-duty-modern_tsej.1920.png) (Credit: Activision)
Today's the day. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, the next big release in Activision's long-running shooter franchise, comes out on October 23, 2026. But if you can't wait that long to get your hands on a new COD, you could sign up for today's Early Access Beta, so you can get a preview of the game's multiplayer mode before everyone else.
How can you get your hands on the game early? You have three options: you can preorder the game to snag an early access code, sign up for Discord Nitro, or play during the open beta.
When Is the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Early Access Beta?
Activision will be holding two separate five-day sessions in August and September, where you can experience the game early. Here's what you need to know:
- Early Access Beta: Early access for Xbox Series X/S, PlayStation 5, and PC will start at 2 p.m. ET / 11 a.m. PT on August 21 and run until 1 p.m. ET / 10 a.m. PT on August 25. You'll need to preorder MW4 to gain access. You can preload the Early Access Beta as early as noon ET / 9 a.m. PT on August 20.
- Open Beta: The game's open beta will then run from 1 p.m. ET / 10 a.m. PT on August 28 to 1 p.m. ET / 10 a.m. PT on September 1 for Xbox, PS5, PC, and Nintendo Switch 2. The Open Beta is available for all players and can be preloaded as early as noon ET / 9 a.m. PT on August 26. You will not need an early access code to play during the Open Beta period.
![](https://sm.pcmag.com/pcmag_uk/photo/c/call-of-du/call-of-duty-modern-warfare-4-beta_tgdv.jpg) (Credit: Activision)
How to Score a Modern Warfare 4 Early Access Beta Code
To actually get a code that will give you access to the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Early Access Beta, you have two options. You can preorder the game or get it through an active Discord Nitro subscription. Here's what you need to know:
Preorder the Game
You can gain access to the Early Access Beta by preordering the game on Xbox, Xbox on PC, PlayStation 5, Battle.net, or Steam. If you buy the game digitally, you won't need a registration code since the Open Beta is available right from platform stores or the in-game store. If you buy a physical edition, the purchase will include an Early Access code that you can redeem online. Once you've signed up and chosen your platform, an Early Access Beta token will be sent via email.
You can preorder from Amazon now:
- Xbox Series X/S and Windows Digital (Standard Edition)
- PlayStation 5 (Standard Edition)
- Xbox Series X (Standard Edition)
Get a Free Discord Nitro Beta Code
An alternative way to access the beta is with an active subscription to Discord Nitro ($9.99 per month). On top of gaining 500MB uploads, custom emoji, unlimited Super Reactions, HD streaming, and server boosts, you'll also gain access to rewards, like Xbox Game Pass and the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 beta. You can claim the beta code from the Nitro Home under the Nitro Rewards section. Once you grab the code, you'll need to redeem it at the Call of Duty website,
Can Your PC Run the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Beta?
Yes, your PC will be able to run the latest Call of Duty beta as long as it meets certain requirements. Here's what your PC should have and what developers recommend"
Minimum System Requirements (PC):
- OS: Windows 10 64 Bit (latest update)
- CPU: AMD Ryzen 5 1600 or Intel Core i5-8400
- RAM: 12GB
- Video Card – AMD: Radeon RX 470
- Video Card – NVIDIA: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 970 / 1060
- Video Card – Intel: Intel Arc A580
- Video Memory: 3 GB
- Storage Space: SSD required
- Network: Broadband Internet connection
- Sound Card: DirectX Compatible
Recommended System Requirements (PC):
- OS: Windows 11 64 Bit (latest update)
- CPU – AMD: AMD Ryzen 5 3600
- CPU – Intel: Intel Core i7-8700
- RAM: 16 GB
- Video Card – AMD: AMD Radeon RX 6700 XT
- Video Card – NVIDIA: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Ti
- Video Card – Intel: Intel Arc B580
- Video Memory: 8 GB
- Storage Space: SSD required
- Network: Broadband Internet connection
- Sound Card: DirectX Compatible
The beta also has specific drivers, shaders, and hardware requirements, so it's worth checking out the Call of Duty website if you have concerns about compatibility issues.
summary: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is scheduled for release on October 23, 2026, with multiplayer beta sessions taking place in August and September. Players can secure early access to the beta by preordering the game or through an active Discord Nitro subscription. An open beta will also be held later in August, which is accessible to all players without a code.
key_points: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 releases on October 23, 2026.
The Early Access Beta runs from August 21 to August 25 and requires a preorder or Discord Nitro subscription.
The Open Beta runs from August 28 to September 1 and is available to all players without a code.
PC players need at least 12GB of RAM, an SSD, and specified CPU and GPU hardware to run the beta.

title: Onimusha: Way of the Sword May Be Another PS5 Capcom Hit as It Crosses 2 Million Wishlists
author: Push Square; Stephen Tailby
content:
![Onimusha: Way of the Sword May Be Another PS5 Capcom Hit as It Crosses 2 Million Wishlists 1](https://images.pushsquare.com/253ffee248d00/onimusha-way-of-the-sword-may-be-another-ps5-capcom-hit-as-it-crosses-2-million-wishlists-1.900x.jpg)
Between Resident Evil Requiem, Pragmata, and Monster Hunter Stories 3, Japanese publisher Capcom has had a super strong 2026, and it looks like its final big game launch of the year could round things out very nicely indeed.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is set to arrive on 4th September, 2026, and while there have been remasters and other offshoots over the years, it will be the first major game in the series since 2006's Onimusha: Dawn of Dreams.
It seems the appetite for a new entry is pretty high, as Capcom has revealed the game has crossed over 2 million wishlists:
Obviously, wishlist numbers don't directly correlate to sales, so this doesn't really guarantee anything. That being said, it does tell us the game is trending well among consumers prior to launch, so it's likely to get off to a good start.
There could be many reasons for the game's wishlist momentum. Onimusha fans who are eager to see the series return, those who enjoy action games in general, and people who have, justifiably, a lot of trust in Capcom may all decide Way of the Sword is worth their attention.
The playable demo certainly helps, and while it drew some criticism for being on the easy side, Capcom has since assured the full game will be tougher.
For what it's worth, assistant editor (and big Onimusha fan) Robert Ramsey played the demo to death back in June and came away feeling very positive.
summary: Capcom's upcoming release "Onimusha: Way of the Sword" has surpassed 2 million wishlists ahead of its September 4, 2026 launch. This marks the first major game in the franchise since 2006, signaling strong consumer interest and momentum. While a recent playable demo received some criticism for being too easy, Capcom has assured players that the full game will feature a higher difficulty.
key_points: Onimusha: Way of the Sword is scheduled to release on September 4, 2026.
The game is the first major entry in the Onimusha series since 2006.
Capcom revealed that the title has crossed 2 million wishlists prior to launch.
A playable demo received criticism for being easy, prompting Capcom to assure a tougher full game.

title: Microsoft has been served a subpoena over 'Grand Theft Auto 6'
author: Jez Corden
content:
![Xbox Series S GTA 6 styled](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/EpffPfhDajDqsqMvwB9qLn.jpg) 
UPDATE (August 21, 2026): Microsoft has responded to the subpoena, with Chief Technical Officer Scott Van Vilet stating: "We are working closely with Take-Two and Rockstar Games to support efforts to protect creative works and intellectual property." Original article continues below.
We are working closely with Take-Two and Rockstar Games to support efforts to protect creative works and intellectual property.August 21, 2026
It hasn't been a fun week if you're working on Grand Theft Auto 6.
GTA is no stranger to controversy, but this year seems to have cranked it up a notch. Take-Two has thrown the rule book out of the window for traditional game launches, and it's to be expected given the scale and hype around GTA 6. People have been waiting well over a decade for a follow up to GTA V, in what promises to be potentially the biggest entertainment launch in history.
Take-Two has raised the ire of long-time fans, however, partially for the price of GTA 6, but also for cutting out standard features and placing them in a $100 edition. Take-Two has also paywalled the first real GTA 6 gameplay footage behind a Netflix subscription, set for premier on August 27, 2026. Then came the hackers.
A self-styled group known as Cyberleeks began spreading footage of GTA 6 on X and other sites last week. The leakers are drip-feeding content from the build, while taking donations in crypto currency. The leaks have knocked Take-Two's share price down 2% over the past week, although it's still up 6% for the year overall. Either way, the firm isn't taking the leaks lying down.
![Grand Theft Auto VI Trailer 2 - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/VQRLujxTm3c/maxresdefault.jpg) 
Shared by Kotaku, the subpeona filed in New York City in the United States, calls on Microsoft, Discord, Google, and others to produce evidence that could lead to the arrest of the leakers.
"The copyrighted material includes but is not limited to audio visual content, artwork, images, dialogue, or other creative elements. Take-Two, through its counsel of record, has submitted a sworn declaration confirming that the purpose for which the DMCA subpoena is sought is to obtain the identity of an alleged infringer or infringers, and that such information will only be used for the purpose of protecting Take-Two’s rights."
"All internal Microsoft business records and investigative records associated with Microsoft’s internal investigation of the ‘cyberleek’ persona sufficient to identify the user(s), person(s) and/or entity/ies associated with that persona."
It's unclear what involvement Microsoft has here directly, although the subpoena suggests Microsoft is conducting an internal investigation of its own into the leaks. There had been some rumors that the GTA 6 builds had emerged from an Xbox dev kit, although it's unclear exactly if that's true right now.
 ![Grand Theft Auto 6 trailer image](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ggCH5JePAkA7e5B9DtSoLB.jpg) 
Either way, Microsoft's vast cloud platform means that it often acts as a first layer of cyber defence for all sorts of companies and even nation states. There's at least some potential here that the Cyberleeks group used or accessed Xbox or Microsoft services in their activities. It could be that the leaked build pings back to Microsoft's Xbox servers, for example, either for uploading telemetry or accessing online services.
Take-Two has also requested information from Discord and Google, and I wouldn't be surprised if they eventually subpoena the crypto exchanges Cyberleeks are using as well.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is set for launch on November 19, 2026, exclusively on Xbox Series X|S and PS5. Other major games have been desperately trying to tailor their launches away from GTA 6, leaving the November launch window somewhat barren.
 ![Click to join us on r/WindowsCentral](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/rX94E5y9uUKpUAhcKF7Ruj.png)

![Jez Corden](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/YzWiDrFEF6Tf6rLJSDy5dD.png)
Jez Corden is the Executive Editor at Windows Central, focusing primarily on all things Xbox and gaming. Jez is known for breaking exclusive news and analysis as relates to the Microsoft ecosystem — while being powered by tea. Follow on X.com/JezCorden and tune in to the XB2 Podcast, all about, you guessed it, Xbox!
