summary: Microsoft has been served a subpoena in New York City regarding recent leaks of "Grand Theft Auto 6" by a group called Cyberleeks. The legal action, driven by Take-Two, seeks evidence and identities of the alleged infringers to protect intellectual property. Microsoft stated it is working closely with Take-Two and Rockstar Games to support these protection efforts.
key_points: Microsoft and other tech companies were served a subpoena to help identify the GTA 6 leakers.
A group called Cyberleeks has been leaking GTA 6 footage online while accepting crypto donations.
Take-Two's subpoena requests internal Microsoft business and investigative records associated with the cyberleek persona.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is scheduled to launch on November 19, 2026, exclusively on Xbox Series X|S and PS5.

title: Microsoft confirms latest Windows 11 update is crashing games and rebooting PCs
author: Kishalaya Kundu
content:
Facepalm: The latest Patch Tuesday update for Windows 11 started rolling out last week, bringing multiple new features, improvements, and bug fixes. However, following several complaints from disgruntled users, Microsoft has now acknowledged that the update may be causing some games to crash on affected devices.
The KB5121003 update was released on August 11 for Windows 11 builds 26200.9168 and 26100.9168. According to some users who installed the update, it contains a bug that is causing games to crash and display the EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION error. In some cases, the PC automatically reboots after the crash.
After Redditor MyCatsNameIsKlaus reported the issue last week, several others confirmed that they were also experiencing crashes, error messages, and random reboots after installing the update. Redditor Thin_Twist7030 even posted event logs, WER reports, and a kernel dump analysis by DeepSeek, suggesting that the game crashes were actually system BSODs that occurred while playing Arc Raiders.
The AI analysis suggests that the problems are caused by a pre-existing "bad-handle bug" that Windows previously ignored or returned an error for when an invalid handle was closed. However, the update appears to have tightened kernel handle validation, causing the same invalid handle close to trigger bug check 0x93 INVALID_KERNEL_HANDLE instead of being tolerated.
![](https://www.techspot.com/images2/news/bigimage/2026/08/2026-08-20-image-27.jpg)
Microsoft confirmed that the issue is affecting Windows 11 versions 25H2 and 24H2 and is investigating whether it is caused by the update or incompatible third-party software. The company added that affected games include Arc Raiders, Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls, and The Finals.
Microsoft hasn't suggested an official workaround, but Thin_Twist7030 claims that rolling back KB5121003 via DISM stopped the crashes on his system. They added that they have paused Windows Update for one month so that the contentious update package won't automatically reinstall. As a permanent fix, they recommend that users remove old drivers responsible for the bad-handle bug.
Game crashes and random reboots are apparently not the only issues caused by KB5121003. According to a Microsoft Learn post by Brian Stringfellow, Teams and the new Outlook are no longer working on Arm devices after installing the update. While Teams crashes after opening, the new Outlook doesn't even launch. The classic Outlook app, however, works as expected.
Stringfellow claims that the issue is affecting a Snapdragon-powered Microsoft Surface Laptop 7th Edition assigned to his company's CFO. He added that the same problem cropped up earlier this year after installing KB5094126, but the issue was resolved by simply rolling back the update. The problem has now apparently reemerged following last week's update.
Microsoft has yet to respond to the report, but a couple of other users replied to the thread, confirming that they are also experiencing similar issues on the HP OmniBook 3 and Surface Pro 11, both powered by Arm64 processors.
summary: Microsoft has confirmed that the recent Windows 11 KB5121003 update is causing game crashes, error messages, and system reboots for users playing titles like Arc Raiders. The update has also broken functionality for Teams and the new Outlook on Arm-powered devices such as the Surface Laptop. Microsoft is currently investigating the issues and whether third-party software is involved, while affected users have found temporary relief by rolling back the update.
key_points: The Windows 11 KB5121003 update causes game crashes and random PC reboots due to a kernel handle validation issue.
Affected games include Arc Raiders, Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls, and The Finals.
Teams and the new Outlook fail to function on Arm-powered devices following the update.
Users have temporarily resolved the issues by rolling back the KB5121003 update using DISM.

title: Geoff Keighley clarifies how trailers are selected for Gamescom Opening Night Live
author: Lewis Packwood
content:
In a press pre-briefing ahead of next week's Gamescom conference, Geoff Keighley has shed some light on the process of how trailers are selected for the Opening Night Live digital showcase, which will take place on Tuesday.
Keighley is also the host of The Game Awards, and in December, Kotaku reported that it allegedly cost up to $450,000 to place a 60-second trailer in the 2025 awards ceremony. Last summer, Aftermath reported that a 60-second trailer in the Keighley-hosted Opening Night Live allegedly cost €102,500 ($119,600).
But in an interview with GamesIndustry.biz last August, Felix Falk, managing director of Game, the German Games Industry Association, said that it was free to place a trailer in Opening Night Live. "Of course, you can place some advertisements in Opening Night Live, but the vast majority of the content is free," he said. "No matter if you're a AAA title or indie, as long as your content is brilliant, Geoff will decide to put you in a show, and it doesn't cost you a penny."
Today, in a Q&A session during the press pre-briefing, GamesIndustry.biz asked Keighley to clarify what it costs to put a trailer in Opening Night Live, and what constitutes an advertisement.
He said that Opening Night Live featured both editorial placements and paid placements. "Much like companies will purchase a booth at Gamescom and buy space, they'll secure space inside of the show," he said.
"One of the things that's important I think to all of us is that there are games that get selected for editorial value in the show. There's also a lot of independent games that we take. You'll see many small teams, games made by three, four people, that get selected to be inside of ONL, because we believe in those titles, and we believe in those teams and want to support them."
He added that these shows are "marketing events, just like Gamescom is a marketing event, so you can consider everything in many ways is marketing video games, but there are definitely games that we select for editorial consideration in all the shows."
GamesIndustry.biz asked for clarification on whether only games that Keighley selects get into Opening Night Live for free, while everyone else has to pay. He replied that it's "a group decision."
"And I would also say the games that are inside, especially ONL, they're all partners to Gamescom in a way. So the companies that we're working with are already at Gamescom in some form as an exhibitor or something like that, and this is maybe a digital extension of what they're doing with their booths."
Falk, who also took part in the pre-briefing, added that "the vast majority of everything we do on the digital side is not paid and is not advertorial or advertisement," and is instead "free for our partners." He said that Gamescom regarded the digital shows as a "hybrid approach" to extend the reach of the event worldwide, "not just addressing those more than 350,000 people on site."
"It's also economically not important for us to make money with the digital shows first, but to give reach to our partners who are at Gamescom," he said.
Keighley also gave some clarification on how games are selected to be editorial placements. "Part of the thing with the editorial selection is really it's the scale of the news or the announcement," he said.
"Everyone wants to tune in to be surprised with something brand new and exciting. Companies and partners often earn the ability to have editorial places with the level of news that people are bringing to the show." But he noted that the show also features "games that are shipping a few weeks later – that's more advertisement of a game that exists."
Keighley confirmed that Gears of War E-Day will be a part of Opening Night Live, along with Final Fantasy 7: Revelation, Ananta, Metro 2039, and more details on the new expansion for The Witcher 3.
Tim Endres, director of Gamescom at Koelnmesse, also noted during the pre-briefing that GDQ (Games Done Quick) will be at Gamescom for the first time this year, raising money for the Gaming for Democracy initiative. "With this, we are using Gamescom once again as a platform for a good cause, and that is really important to us," he said.
Gamescom 2026 is set to be the biggest ever, with nearly 50 pavilions from 40 countries and more than 1,600 exhibitors.
summary: Ahead of the Gamescom Opening Night Live showcase, host Geoff Keighley clarified how trailers are selected and whether they require payment. Keighley explained that the broadcast features a mix of unpaid editorial placements based on news value and paid advertisements. Game, the German Games Industry Association, emphasized that the vast majority of digital content is free for Gamescom partners.
key_points: Opening Night Live includes both editorial placements and paid placements.
Editorial selection is heavily based on the scale of the news or brand-new announcements.
Many independent games are selected for the show for free because organizers believe in the teams.
Felix Falk of the German Games Industry Association stated that the vast majority of digital show content is unpaid for partners.
Gamescom 2026 is slated to feature over 1,600 exhibitors and nearly 50 pavilions from 40 countries.

title: Nintendo wipes out 400 more Switch emulator repositories on GitHub as it continues its fight on piracy | VGC
author: Chris Scullion
content:
![Nintendo wipes out 400 more Switch emulator repositories on GitHub as it continues its fight on piracy](https://www.videogameschronicle.com/files/2021/07/oled-model-photo-03-320x180.jpg)
Nintendo has carried out another round of DMCA takedowns as it continues to fight against Switch emulation.
Back in May 2024 the company took down more than 8,500 clones of Switch emulator Yuzu by issuing a single DMCA notice to GitHub, which led to the site removing 8,535 repositories containing versions of the emulator.
This was followed by another DMCA notice submitted in February 2026, in which Nintendo asked GitHub to take down the repositories still containing Yuzu, as well as those containing at least 12 other Switch emulators.
Now, as reported by TorrentFreak,Â a further seven DMCA notices have been filed by Nintendo, once again asking GitHub to wipe out any instances of Switch emulators on the site.
As a result of these seven DMCA takedown requests, 401 GitHub repositories have been removed, all containing Switch emulators.
The emulator most affected by this is Suyu, one of the more popular successors to the now collapsed Yuzu. Of the 401 repositories removed, 311 of these contained Suyu.
Others removed include Android Switch emulator Skyline, the C#-based MonoNX, and numerous forks of emulators that used Yuzu as a starting point.
Now, if anyone visits any of the 401 GitHub repositories affected, they’re presented with a notice explaining to them that they’ve been taken down, along with a link to the DMCA notice by Nintendo,
“Distribution of these emulators constitutes unlawful trafficking”, Nintendo says
![Nintendo wipes out 400 more Switch emulator repositories on GitHub as it continues its fight on piracy](https://www.videogameschronicle.com/files/2023/02/TLOZ_TearsOfTheKingdom_scrn_25-80x45.jpg)
“The reported repositories offer, link to, or otherwise provide access to Nintendo Switch emulators,” the notice reads. “Nintendo Switch emulators are primarily designed to play Nintendo Switch games. Specifically, these Nintendo Switch emulators illegally circumvent Nintendoâs TPMs in order to run illegal copies of Nintendo Switch games.
“Nintendo Switch games are encrypted using proprietary cryptographic keys (prod.keys) which protect against unauthorized access to and copying of the copyrighted games.
“During operation, the emulators at the reported repositories necessarily use unauthorized copies of these cryptographic keys to decrypt unauthorized copies of Nintendo Switch games, or ROMs, at or immediately before runtime without Nintendoâs authorization.
“Thus, they are primarily designed to and unlawfully ‘circumvent a technological measure that effectively controls access to a work protected under’ the DMCA, and distribution of these emulators constitutes unlawful trafficking in technology that is ‘primarily designed or produced for the purpose of circumventing a technological measure that effectively controls access’ to copyrighted works.
Nintendo sued Yuzu creator Topic Haze in 2024, claiming that The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, was pirated over one million times in the week and a half before its release in May.
Nintendo claimed that Yuzu was “facilitating piracy at a colossal scale”, and Tropic Haze settled the lawsuit just weeks later, agreeing to pay $2.4 million in damages.

The affected projects include Suyu, Skyline, MonoNX, and various Yuzu forks. Nintendo argues that these emulators illegally circumvent its cryptographic technological protection measures to run unauthorized copies of games.
key_points: Nintendo filed seven new DMCA notices resulting in the removal of 401 GitHub repositories containing Switch emulators.
The most affected emulator was Suyu, with 311 of the removed repositories containing the Yuzu successor.
Other impacted repositories included the Android emulator Skyline, MonoNX, and multiple Yuzu forks.
Nintendo asserts that these emulators unlawfully traffic in technology designed to circumvent cryptographic keys and protect copyrighted games.

title: Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 unboxing
author: Ivan
content:
Now that we've welcomed the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 to the office, we can say we've completed the set. And it's a very pink and purple set indeed.
We've got the Galaxy Z Fold8 and Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra reviews over here if you want to check those out, but now let's have a look at the Z Flip8.
The short version is this: Galaxy Z Flip8 is a Galaxy Z Flip7 with a newer chipset and a pink color. We're not sure whether Samsung thinks its flip foldable is perfect or the new market realities meant it may exceed the budget, but it has been unenthusiastic with its upgrades.
So, what is new? The name, obviously! Alright, seriously now, what's different on the eight flip versus the seventh?
The new phone packs newer silicon - either the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in the US, Canada, and China, or the Exynos 2600 in most other places. Its two screens are also slightly brighter - 3,000 nits vs 2,600 nits.
![It has the same cover display, only a bit brighter](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/08/samsung-galaxy-z-flip8-ifr/-326/gsmarena_002.jpg) 
![It has the same cover display, only a bit brighter](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/08/samsung-galaxy-z-flip8-ifr/-326/gsmarena_003.jpg) 
It has the same cover display, only a bit brighter
The pink color is also new and suits the phone and its form factor just right! We've never had any complaints when it comes to the Galaxy Z Flip's build quality and in-hand feel, and this one is not going to change that.
![Now comes in Pink, which is nice](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/08/samsung-galaxy-z-flip8-ifr/-326/gsmarena_004.jpg) 
![Now comes in Pink, which is nice](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/08/samsung-galaxy-z-flip8-ifr/-326/gsmarena_005.jpg) 
Now comes in Pink, which is nice
The rest of the phone is essentially the same - the displays, the battery, the charging speed, even the cameras. If you're a Galaxy Z Flip7 owner, you need not worry about upgrading.
For everyone else the Galaxy Z Flip8 remains a great little phone. Just like the rest of the foldable Galaxy lineup, it's polished and has a very upmarket feel to it. That goes for more than just the hardware. Samsung's software experience is very smooth, fully functional, and sort of refreshing. It's not just another iOS clone.
![Displays are great, but the cover screen isn't LTPO](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/08/samsung-galaxy-z-flip8-ifr/-326/gsmarena_006.jpg) 
![Displays are great, but the cover screen isn't LTPO](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/08/samsung-galaxy-z-flip8-ifr/-326/gsmarena_007.jpg) 
Displays are great, but the cover screen isn't LTPO 
The Galaxy Z Flip8 comes in either 12/256GB or 12/512GB. It can be clad in Cream, Graphite, and Pink, as well as an online-exclusive Mint color. It starts from €1,300 (though it's currently 32% off).

title: Psychonauts Dev Double Fine Will Let You Decide What Game It Makes Next
author: Push Square; Liam Croft
content:
![Brutal Legend PS3](https://images.pushsquare.com/f3a905857be5f/brutal-legend-ps3.900x.jpg)
Update []:
Double Fine has announced Amnesia Fortnight 2026, a Kickstarter page that'll let you help decide what the developer makes next.
It's putting on a live game jam, and of the ideas the developers come up with, the people who support the Kickstarter will select four to be made into prototypes. From there, one of those four prototypes will be picked to become an actual game Double Fine creates.
The Kickstarter will launch on 31st August 2026. Here's the idea in the studio's own words:
We're going to do a Game Jam, live on the internet, in which our backers will get to choose which of our myriad of ideas get made into four new prototypes — and which of those final four will become a real (small) game. You may even snag some sweet merchables and rarities along the way.
Original Story: Psychonauts team Double Fine is going to share "what's next for the studio" today as part of a livestream on the Kinda Funny Games YouTube channel.
Having just returned to independence after years of ownership under Microsoft, the developer plans to talk about its future on the live show scheduled to start in the coming hours. I doubt you're going to get actual game announcements out of the livestream, but I presume Tim Schafer will be there to talk about how Double Fine will approach its future.
Whatever happens, I'll update this article with the news.
At the end of last month, 23 employees had to be let go from Double Fine in order to ensure the team's future. "As a small, tightly-knit team, these actions are not taken lightly. Only the survival of our studio would ever make us consider such a painful action. Our transition to becoming an independent company also means becoming a size that we can sustain," Schafer said.
summary: Developer Double Fine has announced Amnesia Fortnight 2026, a Kickstarter campaign allowing backers to vote on game ideas created during a live game jam. Backers will select four ideas to become prototypes, and one of those prototypes will be developed into a full game. The studio recently returned to independence after Microsoft's ownership and laid off 23 employees to ensure the studio's long-term survival.
key_points: Double Fine announced Amnesia Fortnight 2026 via a Kickstarter page launching on August 31, 2026.
Backers will vote on developer ideas from a live game jam to choose four prototypes.
One of the four prototypes will be developed into a real game.
The studio recently returned to independence after years under Microsoft ownership.
Double Fine laid off 23 employees at the end of last month to ensure the studio's sustainability as an independent company.

title: The Blood Of Dawnwalker Has Two Performance Modes On Xbox Series X, But No 60FPS
author: Pure Xbox; Craig Reid
content:
We've timestamped the gameplay trailer to start at the beginning of the Xbox Series X performance mode specifications.
Rebel Wolves has posted Xbox Series X gameplay for its upcoming RPG, The Blood of Dawnwalker, revealing the two graphical modes you can expect when it launches on Xbox and other platforms on September 3rd.
The trailer features PS5 Pro, PS5 and Xbox Series X gameplay, with the obvious stinker being that none of the consoles will support 60FPS. Instead, Xbox Series X will offer 30FPS and 40FPS modes. Here's what you can expect:
| Category | Quality | Balanced | 
|---|---|---|
| Resolution | Dynamic 4K | Dynamic 4K | 
| Frames Per Second | 30FPS | 40FPS | 
It's a surprise to see a game launching in 2026 on Microsoft's flagship console without a 60FPS option. The trailer doesn't reveal any details about the less powerful Xbox Series S either. Perhaps most bizarrely, even the PS5 Pro doesn't appear to support 60FPS.
The upcoming RPG is being spun up by some of the old hats behind the incredible Witcher 3, and judging from early previews The Blood of Dawnwalker is certainly worth keeping your eye on - even if it's lacking those extra frames.
So, is the lack of a dedicated 60FPS mode a deal breaker for you? Make sure to vote in the poll below and talk to us about it in the comments section.
summary: Rebel Wolves has revealed that its upcoming RPG, The Blood of Dawnwalker, will not feature a 60FPS mode on consoles when it launches on September 3. Instead, the Xbox Series X will provide two graphical options: a Quality mode running at Dynamic 4K and 30FPS, and a Balanced mode running at Dynamic 4K and 40FPS. Even more powerful systems, including the PS5 Pro, reportedly lack 60FPS support.
key_points: The Blood of Dawnwalker launches on September 3 on Xbox and other platforms.
Xbox Series X offers two modes: Quality (Dynamic 4K at 30FPS) and Balanced (Dynamic 4K at 40FPS).
None of the consoles, including the PS5 Pro, support a 60FPS mode.
The trailer provided no performance details for the Xbox Series S.

title: The Blood of Dawnwalker Won't Have 60FPS Mode on PS5 or Even PS5 Pro
author: Push Square; Liam Croft
content:
Rebel Wolves has announced the graphical modes you can pick between in The Blood of Dawnwalker, and the standout news is that neither of the two settings provided offers 60 frames-per-second support on base PS5 or PS5 Pro.
On both base PS5 and PS5 Pro, there are the same two modes to choose from:
- Quality
- Dynamic 4K, Targeting 30 FPS
- Balanced
- Dynamic 4K, Targeting 40FPS
The video above notes the PS5 Pro "offers enhanced visual quality across both modes", but there's seemingly no way of making the console version run at 60fps.
![YouTube Video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/y-XGB8_bQ3s/maxresdefault.jpg) Watch on
Subscribe to Push Square on YouTube171k
It's a surprise to see a PS5 game in 2026 not offer any kind of 60fps support, especially when it has multiple graphics modes to toggle between. I find it strange how there's even a mode named "Balanced" — how can it be balanced between anything when there's no performance mode to accompany the quality mode? A balanced mode usually sits in between the two, but that's not the case here.
summary: Developer Rebel Wolves has announced that The Blood of Dawnwalker will not feature a 60 frames-per-second mode on either the base PlayStation 5 or the PS5 Pro. Players will instead choose between a Quality mode targeting 30 FPS and a Balanced mode targeting 40 FPS, with both utilizing dynamic 4K resolution. The inclusion of these modes without a 60 FPS option has surprised observers, particularly given the absence of a dedicated performance mode.
key_points: The Blood of Dawnwalker lacks 60 FPS support on both the base PS5 and PS5 Pro.
The game offers two graphical settings: Quality (targeting 30 FPS) and Balanced (targeting 40 FPS).
Both available graphical modes utilize dynamic 4K resolution.
The PS5 Pro version provides enhanced visual quality across both modes.

title: I thought Metal Gear Solid 4 had aged badly – playing it on PS5 changed my mind
author: Ian Dean
content:
Our Verdict
MGS4 remains an ambitious, gloriously excessive finale, and Vol. 2 gives it the modern platform it deserves, despite some dated design choices, lengthy cutscenes and uneven representation. Ghost Babel, Peace Walker, and deep-cut extras round out a good package.
For
- MGS4 is finally playable again
- Ghost Babel is a pixel art joy
- Excellent extras and fan service
Against
- Some design choices haven't aged
Why you can trust Creative Bloq
 ![Old Snake and Snake in the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 key art](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/gkdaYxEvVzYHsY5YzsQBZm.jpg) 
Publisher Konami
Developer Konami / Kojima Productions
Release date 27 August
Format PlayStation 5 (reviewed), Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, PC
Platform Proprietary / Unity (menus) / Unreal Engine 5 (Database)
Playing Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots for the first time since it launched back in 2008 is a strange feeling, partly because so much of what made it feel enormous back then has simply disappeared from games, that sense that you're playing the latest instalment in some sprawling, decades-long saga where every character, conspiracy and elegant bit of military hardware has been building towards this one enormous finale.
We get big games now, obviously, GTA6 is nearly here, but very few arrive carrying quite this much baggage, and MGS4 doesn't exactly try to hide it either, it throws the whole lot at you: Big Boss, Liquid, the Patriots, Snake's ageing, the Beauty and the Beast Unit, a return to Shadow Moses, Metal Gear REX, Ocelot pulling strings, and somehow expects you to keep up.
Then, when the music swells, and Old Snake is crawling towards his end, tapping 'Triangle' to keep him alive and save the world, it still works. I know what's coming, I've played it before, I've spent enough time with the series to know where all of this is heading, and yet there's something about seeing Old Snake drag himself towards his final confrontation that remains truly epic.
That might be the strangest thing about coming back to MGS4 in 2026, and it's fantastic that we finally can, because for all the things that have aged badly, and there are plenty, Kojima's finale still has an extraordinary sense of occasion, playfulness and invention that many modern games simply don't have or strive for.
 ![Screens from MGS4 in Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ANSJFk3euczUpNgFyaxMg6.jpg) 
MGS4 is playable again
It also helps that this is the first time I've been able to play it properly outside the PS3, and it still feels like a technical triumph. MGS4 was already pushing the PS3 hard in 2008, and I had forgotten just how much visual information it was trying to throw around. The Middle Eastern battlefields are still busy and grimy, the character models hold up surprisingly well, the snow blowing around Shadow Moses looks fantastic, and the Shadow Moses Metal Gear encounter remains an enormous technical showcase designed to sell you on the power of PS3. There's not really a drop in quality from what you watch and what you play, and while that seems a given these days, in 2008 it felt like magic.
At 4K and 60fps it feels clean and crisp without losing that slightly grubby late-PS3 character, and while the assets obviously haven't been rebuilt to modern standards, the actual design has aged far better than I expected. The enemy design, environments and boss encounters still have nuance and subtle ideas running through them, rather than simply being places to walk through or fight between cinematics; designs like the Gekko that mix machine and organic, muscle, that 'moo' like cows and hunt in packs exude personality and showcase Kojima's renowned attention to detail.
 ![Screens from MGS4 in Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/2fcqPssDvAugiAJAme3j27.jpg) 
The Beauty and the Beast Unit are still one of the best examples of this. These bosses are women traumatised by war and turned into machines of destruction, revenge and spectacle, and yes, the way MGS4 presents them is very much tied to the late 2000s, with Kojima's fascination with sex, violence and fetishised character design often pushing things further than they need to go, and in fact even 18 years ago eyesbrows were raised, but mechanically they're memorable fights that bookend missions nicely while playing on nostalgia for earlier entries in the series.
Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.
Laughing Octopus can camouflage herself into the scenery and disappear into rooms you've just searched, firing clouds of ink that disorient Snake, while Night Vision gives you another way of tracking her by picking up the footprints she leaves behind. Screaming Mantis takes control of dead as well as living soldiers, and Meryl's presence gives you another perilous route through the encounter as she's used as a human shield, particularly once you realise that shooting Mantis' puppets can help break through her defences. They are weird, inventive fights and, importantly, they make you think for a few minutes before you get to go back to the next enormous cinematic.
Because yes, that problem is still here. Back in 2008, I remember feeling that the balance between actually playing MGS4 and watching MGS4 was a little off, and coming back to it now hasn't changed my mind. You can play for a handful of minutes, and then suddenly you're watching a 20-minute cinematic, particularly during the early stages, and although the story is doing important work, it can feel like the controller has been taken away just when you're getting into the rhythm of the game.
 ![Screens from MGS4 in Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/FVvZNxfkuMTdMSVwLsrum6.jpg) 
Do want an MGS lore dump?
That isn't helped by the sheer amount of lore you're expected to soak up and ponder upon. MGS4 is assuming you've followed Snake from the original Metal Gear through Metal Gear 2, MGS1 and MGS2, and then spent enough time thinking about Big Boss, Zero, the Patriots, Liquid, Ocelot and the various clone projects to remember who everyone is when they suddenly appear on screen. If you've only a passing relationship with Metal Gear, good luck.
But if you have followed it, the fan service is ridiculous, and that's really why you were here in 2008 anyway. The final third is still one of the most effective pieces of nostalgia bait I've seen in a game, whether it's pressing 'X' during scenes to recall iconic moments or the iconic mission that starts with a pixel-art dream sequence before sending Snake back to Shadow Moses, the setting of the original Metal Gear Solid. It is basically Kojima taking you by the hand and walking you around his own history, pointing at things you remember and then nudging you to make sure you noticed the reference.
There are jokes about changing discs, because in Metal Gear Solid on PS1 you had to swap discs at this precise moment, and now you're on a PS5, so there's no need (the joke is edited from the PS3 original). The ghost of Psycho Mantis gets another fourth-wall-breaking shot at messing with you, only to discover there's no memory card for him to read, before settling for making the DualSense vibrate very weakly instead. It's silly, it's completely unnecessary, and it works because Metal Gear has always understood that the player is part of the joke.
Kojima spends much of the game doing things like this, breaking the fourth wall and turning the hardware itself into part of the experience. The controller can vibrate, and inputs become erratic to make you feel Old Snake's distress; Beauty and the Beast bosses 'remember' past encounters, while Snake can destress by reading Playboy magazines found in missions, which feels particularly funny now because it is such an aggressively 2000s idea of what a video game soldier should be doing.
 ![Screens from MGS4 in Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/QmYGoCfnG9hsJFajbyi2v6.jpg) 
Other moments haven't aged nearly as well. Snake staring at Naomi's chest affects his stress meter, and the game's treatment of its female characters can veer between genuinely interesting and deeply uncomfortable, sometimes within the same encounter (Mei Ling is the butt of one too many jokes). The Beauty and the Beast Unit are tragic products of war and fascinating mechanical opponents, but the camera and character designs are still very much Kojima circa 2008.
It's a game of contradictions like that, really, and perhaps that's why it remains so fascinating. For all the talking, MGS4 has some superb gameplay when it lets you get on with it. The return to Shadow Moses is fantastic, the sniper sequence in the snowstorm works brilliantly, the Metal Gear battle is a spectacular showcase, and the motorbike chase through an Eastern Europe Prague-inspired city is the sort of hyperactive cinematic set piece that makes you forget about the tedious cat-and-mouse follow-the-spy section that comes before it.
The enemy and world design have held up especially well, because Kojima's team has always been good at making the game's mechanics feel like part of the world rather than systems sitting on top of it. You aren't just shooting enemies; you're dealing with soldiers whose behaviour changes depending on the battlefield, watching factions fight each other, manipulating it too, and finding ways to move through spaces where the chaos can sometimes work in your favour, even now, which makes MGS4 unique.
Then I remember that this was all happening on the PS3 and you really need to admire the creative work involved. It's easy to look at the 4K/60fps presentation and assume the game has been substantially rebuilt, but this is still the MGS4 you remember. Konami hasn't recreated it in Unreal Engine 5 like Metal Gear Solid Delta: Snake Eater, and the underlying art and animation still come from the original game. What you're getting is a modern port and presentation of that 2008 game, and that's enough because the design still works, and it has one of the best final thirds of any game you'll play this year.
![A screen from Peace Walker, Snake, Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/WAvNvxLKMMQ3cTHbYMh684-1200-80.png) 
![Screens from Peace Walker HD](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/UsdHVPjDMDTg6PMhFRYFBL-1200-80.png) 
![Screens from Peace Walker HD](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/H9bmEP5yr6UAmKSAhzwfAL-1200-80.png) 
![Screens from Peace Walker HD](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/bRJVsRuv6K7iQgoXfFxWBL-1200-80.png) 
![A screen from Peace Walker, Snake, Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/WAvNvxLKMMQ3cTHbYMh684-1280-80.png) 
![Screens from Peace Walker HD](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/UsdHVPjDMDTg6PMhFRYFBL-1280-80.png) 
![Screens from Peace Walker HD](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/H9bmEP5yr6UAmKSAhzwfAL-1280-80.png) 
![Screens from Peace Walker HD](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/bRJVsRuv6K7iQgoXfFxWBL-1280-80.png) 
Peace Walker and Ghost Babel
The rest of Master Collection Vol. 2 is almost a relief after all of that. Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker is the obvious second headline game, originally released on PSP and set during Big Boss's story after MGS3: Snake Eater. It's a very different kind of Metal Gear, built around short missions and the gradual development of Mother Base, where you can transport enemy soldiers and equipment back to your operation (using comical balloons), expand your private military force and build up the resources you need for later missions.
I remembered liking the idea of Peace Walker more than the actual game, but it works better on PS5 than I expected. Those bite-sized missions, originally designed for a handheld, suit modern pick-up-and-play sessions surprisingly well, and the HD version runs at 60fps; the underlying assets still have their PSP origins, but the character models look sharp on a large TV.
The art does a lot of work here to sell Peace Walker's personality. Yoji Shinkawa's expressive, ink-heavy style remains one of the series' strongest parts, and the comic-panel cutscenes painted by Ashley Wood look particularly good because they were designed around these illustrations rather than trying to pretend the PSP could deliver MGS4-style cinematics. They can look a little blurry and blown-out on a TV, but the interactive elements are still fun – shooting mechs and fighting enemies inside comic panels is a very fourth-wall-breaking addition to the series.
But there is heavy asset reuse, and you will return to the environments time and again to grind for resources, which was always an issue with Peace Walker on PSP. As a handheld game, it worked because we accept the restrictions; here it can get repetitive, with only the lore to keep you hooked, because as with every Kojima game, there are big twists, teases, and insights that lead into other areas of the series.
 ![Art from Peace Walker](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ZCKkqdZRJtZjUuWoWdDxs9.png) 
Then there's Metal Gear: Ghost Babel, the Game Boy Color game that is arguably the purest Metal Gear experience in the whole collection, and the one game that disconnects from Kojima's need to keep fleshing out the Snake saga's lore, because it's set in an alternate timeline. Despite its Western title, Metal Gear Solid isn't a Game Boy version of the PlayStation game. It's an original story built specifically around the Game Boy Color, and that gives it a lovely sense of identity rather than feeling like a compromised version of something bigger. For that reason, and its simple, direct game design, Ghost Babel is a really enjoyable entry.
That sounds like a big statement when you sit it alongside Guns of the Patriots, but after hours of Snake's ageing, the Patriots, Liquid Ocelot and enough exposition to fill several textbooks – which funnily enough are, kind of, included here as the original scripts – playing this pixel art 2D stealth game feels fantastic. You sneak around, avoid guards, collect keycards, find routes and puzzle-solve through maze-like environments and generally get on with playing rather than being told about the history of the Metal Gear universe.
There is something refreshing about seeing Metal Gear reduced to those basic ingredients again, especially after replaying MGS4. And while it's basic, there are still moments of inspiration – boss fights like trap-based Black Arts Viper that require some thought to defeat – and nice touches like hiding in water and grass, tapping to lure enemies, basically all the stealth ideas from the 3D series distilled into pixels.
 ![MG Ghost Babel screen](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ZWF9rXYrzUFJP4hmikftjU.jpg) 
The Master Collection Vol. 2 extras
Master Collection Vol. 2 also goes far beyond simply putting three games on a disc. It includes the MGS4 and Peace Walker Screenplay Books, Master Books covering characters and story information, the MGS4 Database, a digital soundtrack, and other archive material. The wealth of content is fitting too, because Metal Gear has always been as much about its world-building as its gameplay, and being able to dig into that material makes Master Collection Vol. 2 feel more like an archive than a simple rerelease. Presentation is excellent too, with nice photography and clean menu designs, and you can adjust screen settings and dimensions if you want, such as pixel smoothing in Ghost Babel.
Compared with Master Collection Vol. 1 at launch, the PS5 version of Vol.2 feels considerably more polished. I'm not seeing the same combination of low-resolution presentation, 30fps limitations, input problems and obvious bugs that made the first collection feel like it needed more time before release. For Master Collection Vol. 2, it's simply the games that catch the eye.
 ![A book page from Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/7gTL2Amsc9B7rcCV9yvg6j.jpg) 
That's the biggest surprise here, because I went back into MGS4 expecting to be reminded why I didn't love it so much in 2008, and in some ways I was surprised by how modern it actually feels to play and replay on PS5; I enjoyed it more. The cutscenes are still very long, the exposition bloated, some of the sexual representation has aged badly, and the game assumes you care deeply about a story that has been running since 1987.
But I also remembered why I cared about it in the first place: I had to play it at the time, and enjoy replaying it again now. MGS4 has an ambition you rarely see now: a willingness to let a video game become completely consumed by its own history, then try to bring all of it to a close. It can be exhausting, occasionally embarrassing and sometimes completely baffling, but when the pieces come together it still has an emotional force that's difficult to dismiss.
Peace Walker gives the collection a much more manageable stealth-action experience, and Ghost Babel is a wonderful reminder of how simple and inventive Metal Gear could be before Kojima turned the series into his own particular blend of video game, action movie, political thriller and elaborate in-joke.
But if you're buying Master Collection Vol. 2, you're buying it for MGS4, and after 18 years, finally being able to play that game outside the PS3, in 4K and at 60fps, running nicely, it's worth the price of admission. Whatever you thought of Old/Solid Snake's final mission in 2008, there's something genuinely satisfying about watching it run properly on a modern console, especially when the music starts, the callbacks begin piling up, and you realise you're heading towards that ending all over again.
I still don't think MGS4 is the best Metal Gear game, but playing it again has reminded me why it felt like such a big deal back in 2008.
out of 10
MGS4 remains an ambitious, gloriously excessive finale, and Vol. 2 gives it the modern platform it deserves, despite some dated design choices, lengthy cutscenes and uneven representation. Ghost Babel, Peace Walker, and deep-cut extras round out a good package.
![Ian Dean](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/quozhVpr48BAH6CBd6saBg.jpg)
Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

summary: Metal Gear Solid 4 remains an ambitious, excessive finale that retains an extraordinary sense of occasion when played on modern hardware through the Master Collection Vol. 2. While some elements like lengthy cutscenes, heavy lore dumps, and dated late-2000s character tropes have not aged well, the game's inventive mechanics, technical presentation at 4K/60fps, and clever fan service still hold up. The package is rounded out by other titles like Peace Walker and Ghost Babel, making the classic experience playable on modern platforms.
key_points: MGS4 is finally playable outside of the PS3 through the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2, running at 4K and 60fps.
The game retains its signature contradictions, featuring brilliant enemy design and mechanical inventiveness alongside overly long cinematics and dated female character depictions.
Extensive fan service and nostalgia-driven moments, such as the return to Shadow Moses and fourth-wall-breaking jokes, remain highlights of the experience.
The collection also includes other titles like Peace Walker and Ghost Babel, which benefit from the modern platform and shorter mission designs.

title: Aliens at 40: from wearable cameras to exoskeletons, here are the technologies the film predicted
author: Steve Benford
content:
Director James Cameron’s acclaimed sci-fi movie Aliens turns 40 in August. It’s a sequel to Ridley Scott’s claustrophobic breakout hit Alien, made in 1979. Where the original featured one terrifying creature, Cameron’s movie features hundreds – and pits them against a squad of space marines.
A host of intriguing technologies make an appearance, including interstellar travel, hypersleep (where humans are preserved in stasis for long space journeys) and terraforming (making other worlds liveable for humans).
Some of the technologies in the film have already come to pass – or look likely to soon. But others were missed and some remain firmly in the realms of science fiction.
In Aliens, the marines travel to a distant moon to investigate the disappearance of over 100 human settlers. Ellen Ripley (Sigourney Weaver), the main protagonist of the first film, goes along to advise.
On arrival, they run into a six-year-old girl, called Newt, who managed to escape the grisly fate of the other colonists. When the marines encounter the alien hive, chaos and carnage ensue.
The technology featured in Aliens appears to be there to support the wonderful storytelling, rather than predict the path of innovation, as a futurologist might.
But let’s take a look at it. The film is set in 2179, 153 years into our future. Journeying 153 years into the past would land us in 1893, when common technologies were horse drawn and steam streetcars and gas lighting. Typewriters with Qwerty keyboards went on sale the following year.
Industrial aesthetic
We’ve moved on considerably, but the future world of Aliens feels less distant in many respects. Company executives use clunky business cards to trigger low-resolution video calls and wave computer printouts during meeting room showdowns.
For modern audiences, however, the lack of personal electronic devices may be jarring. One can only assume that they must have fallen out of favour by 2179.
The gritty, industrial visual style established in the first film was taken further here. Aliens introduces a variety of military vehicles that contain futuristic elements while drawing on real hardware used in the Vietnam war. The movie’s look influenced later films, but it has also been described as “everyday” and “ugly”.
An exception is the tracking technology: the motion detectors, wearable cameras and biosensors embedded into wristbands. These feel broadly “current”. But if we extrapolate from the present day, one might expect engineers in 2179 to make greater use of surveillance cameras and computer vision (a sub-field of AI where machines are trained to “understand” images and video).
A network of “smart cameras” throughout the moon colony could have tracked both the aliens and humans. Similar networks today monitor crowds and individuals – and watch for suspicious behaviour – on city streets and public transport.
Sentry guns and exoskeletons
The robots of Aliens are striking. Some are not so far removed from hardware used today, but with notable differences. In two separate scenes, Ripley straps into a massive mechanical suit known as a “loader”.
They are mainly used to move cargo, but, conveniently, can be appropriated for fighting xenomorphs. The loaders are a type of exoskeleton, real life wearable tech that may enhance human strength or movement.
Exoskeletons aren’t generally used for this kind of task yet. Large autonomous or teleoperated factory robots are the go-to technology for lifting heavy hardware. This is safer than having humans operate in such hazardous environments.
Current exoskeletons are smaller in scale than the loaders. They are helping people walk again after traumatic injury and commercial versions are available to support those with mobility issues to hill walk.
The war in Ukraine, meanwhile, has familiarised us with autonomous combat robots. One or two share a striking resemblance to the film’s automated sentry guns, which guard an entrance passage in the colony. But drone aircraft, in heavy use today, are notable by their absence.
However, one robot in Aliens operates at a level far beyond the rest: the android Bishop, played by Lance Henriksen. Bishop looks like a human on the outside and is referred to in the film as a “synthetic”.
By 2179, synthetics appear to be approaching human levels of cognitive function – something known as artificial general intelligence (AGI). They even seem to observe the laws of robotics devised by scientist and author Isaac Asimov. In one scene, Bishop tells crew members that he cannot harm a human or allow one to be harmed – Asimov’s first law.
Synthetics occupy capable and realistic bodies which seem to incorporate soft robotics. In this real research area, scientists create robots with flexible materials instead of hard ones, such as metal. Fluids or pressurised air generate movement rather than conventional electric actuators.
The synthetics probably have soft robotic systems overlaid on a rigid framework, similar to flesh on bone. They are therefore likely to be a mixture of soft and conventional robotics.
Tech conundrum
Some of the tech in Aliens remains well out of reach. We don’t have propulsion systems capable of sending crews to other stars and back within a lifetime. As regards hypersleep, in rare cases, humans have survived extreme hypothermia for over an hour, but this is not recommended. Terraforming, meanwhile, remains resolutely theoretical. But what of the synthetics?
Rightly or wrongly, many researchers and companies aspire to create humanoid robots and achieve AGI. We are bombarded with visions of their latest efforts on social media. But some proportion of those working on such ventures are looking to raise money. Many experts would argue that synthetic humans like those in the Alien movies are still far beyond today’s capabilities.
This leads us to a striking conundrum at the heart of Aliens. Why aren’t there more synthetics? Why not send a population of them to terraform worlds or fight aggressive ETs?
Perhaps humans are more expendable: maybe we will end up doing AI’s dirty work because we are the cheaper commodity. But there is a more optimistic answer. Maybe, despite all of our apparent failings and weaknesses, humans are the more capable being.
After all, it is Ripley – not Bishop – who, wildly improvising with available technologies and driven by her unstoppable desire to protect Newt, defeats the alien queen. Perhaps there is hope yet for our species.
summary: James Cameron's 1986 film Aliens features a variety of futuristic technologies, some of which have paralleled modern advancements while others remain in science fiction. While the movie successfully predicted elements like wearable cameras, motion detectors, exoskeletons, and automated sentry guns, technologies such as interstellar travel, hypersleep, and true artificial general intelligence remain out of reach. The film's industrial aesthetic notably lacks personal electronic devices and modern surveillance networks, yet highlights the enduring capability of humans over machines.
key_points: The 1986 film Aliens turns 40 in August and depicts numerous technologies ranging from interstellar travel to exoskeletons.
Some technologies shown in the film have materialized today, including motion detectors, wearable cameras, biosensors, and exoskeletons.
Other prominent technologies from the movie, such as interstellar propulsion, hypersleep, and terraforming, remain theoretical or impossible.
The film's advanced android, Bishop, showcases features resembling artificial general intelligence and soft robotics, though human-like synthetics are still far beyond current capabilities.
Despite featuring advanced machinery and automated sentry guns, the film notably lacks modern personal electronic devices and drone aircraft.

title: Call Of Duty: MW4 Open Beta Dates, Start Times & How To Download
author: Pure Xbox; Fraser Gilbert
content:
It's almost time for the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 (MW4) Open Beta! With the full game set to release this October, the beta will provide your first chance to check out not only the multiplayer, but even a sample of the campaign as well.
So, here's a look at everything you need to know about the Modern Warfare 4 / MW4 Open Beta:
Call Of Duty MW4 Beta: Dates And Start Times
The Modern Warfare 4 Open Beta goes ahead on two upcoming weekends. The first weekend is for pre-orders only (Game Pass doesn't count this year), with a second open beta to follow for all players.
The first early access beta weekend begins August 21st and lasts until August 25th.
The second open beta weekend will then follow on August 28th and conclude on September 1st.
Official start times for the early access beta weekend are as follows:
- North America: 11am PDT / 12pm MDT / 1pm CDT / 2pm EDT
- UK/Ire: 7pm BST
- Europe: 8pm CEST / 9pm EEST
- Asia/Oceania: 3am (Sat) JST / 2am (Sat) AWST / 4am (Sat) AEST
Official start times for the second open beta weekend are as follows:
- North America: 10am PDT / 11am MDT / 12pm CDT / 1pm EDT
- UK/Ire: 6pm BST
- Europe: 7pm CEST / 8pm EEST
- Asia/Oceania: 2am (Sat) JST / 1am (Sat) AWST / 3am (Sat) AEST
summary: The Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 open beta offers players a preview of the multiplayer and campaign ahead of the full game's October release. The beta takes place across two weekends, beginning with an early access period for pre-orders from August 21 to August 25. A second open beta for all players will follow from August 28 to September 1.
key_points: The full game is scheduled to release this October.
The first beta weekend runs from August 21st to August 25th and is restricted to pre-orders.
Game Pass subscriptions do not count for early access this year.
The second beta weekend runs from August 28th to September 1st and is open to all players.
Both weekends feature specific regional start times.

title: Google Home update lets you set light color temperature to your favorite kelvin using voice commands
author: Andrew Romero
content:
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/06/Google-Home-Speaker-2.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1600) 
Google Home is rolling out an update that addresses some of the most overlooked pain points for the voice assistant, like refined broadcast commands, better Spotify request recognition, and granular smart light color temperature control down to the kelvin. Don’t be shy; we all have a favorite kelvin rating.
Google has been rolling out quality Home updates in a steady stream recently. Most of the updates focus on improvements to Gemini for Home and the polish that’s needed since it’s still stuck in early access. Today’s update, though, is bringing some solid changes to issues that have plagued even the lightest Google Home users.
The August 20 update includes three changes to the Google Home voice assistant – Gemini. First, Spotify command recognition has reportedly been cleaned up. Google says it’s “improved how [it] recognize[s] the songs, artists, and playlists you request on Spotify.” For the seasoned Google Home users, requests for certain songs have always been a little hit or miss. Further, general voice commands often get mistaken for music requests, and random tunes begin to play at an uncomfortable volume. Hopefully, this update lessens that occurrence.
Changes to how broadcasts are handled is packed into the changelog, too. Google notes that broadcasts will now be a two-step process. You ask for Gemini to broadcast a message, wait, then let it know what the message is. Much better than the one-line request prone to miscommunication.
The last voice assistant change will make the color temperature nerds happy. Google Home will now recognize voice commands with specific color temperature requests. You can say “Hey Google, set the living room lights to 2700 kelvins,” and you’ll get an accurate color shift. This has always been an option in the app, but not something easily done with voice controls. You may need to learn color temperature ratings by heart.
The changelog adds that several adjustments are taking place in the app, like consistent temperature unit of measurements across all devices. European-style door locks are gaining support, as well.
Google says there should be fewer app crashes on iOS devices and better offline camera controls that remain consistent during connection issues. This comes after Google recently added support for more third-party cameras.
On Android, the update fixes an issue where camera streams could get stuck at 360p. If the connection allows, affected cameras should stream at full resolution.
Lastly, failed payments for Google Home Premium will result in a clear alert, so there isn’t a lapse in features or camera storage.
Google’s August 20 update for Google Home should be rolling out to users starting today.
![Add 9to5Google as a preferred source on Google](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/themes/ninetofive/dist/images/google-preferred-source-badge-dark.png) 
![Add 9to5Google as a preferred source on Google](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/themes/ninetofive/dist/images/google-preferred-source-badge-light.png)
summary: Google is rolling out an August 20 update for Google Home that introduces several improvements to voice assistant commands and app functionality. The update features better Spotify request recognition, a new two-step process for broadcasts, and the ability to control smart light color temperatures using specific kelvin values via voice. Additional fixes address iOS app crashes, Android camera streaming resolution, offline camera controls, and payment alerts for Google Home Premium.
key_points: Google Home now recognizes specific color temperature requests down to the kelvin via voice commands.
Spotify request recognition has been improved to reduce errors and unintended music playback.
Broadcasts have been updated to a two-step process where users ask Gemini to broadcast and then provide the message.
The update includes fixes for iOS app crashes and resolves an Android issue where camera streams got stuck at 360p.
Failed payments for Google Home Premium will now trigger a clear alert to prevent a lapse in features.

title: FromSoftware has closed down the first day of The Duskblood's network test early due to connectivity issues
author: Connor Makar
content:
UPDATE 2PM BST: FormSoftware has closed today's The Duskbloods network test early due to connectivity issues.
In a statement made on the official FromSoftware X account, the company announced the news and said it would share future testing schedules soon.
![Cover image for YouTube video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/dMrTr9cz53k/hqdefault.jpg) The Duskbloods - Official Closed Network Test Trailer | Nintendo Direct June 2026
"We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience caused to those who were waiting for the first The Duskbloods network test due to game server issues," the statement read. "We regret to inform you that today's session is now closed. We will continue to work on improving the servers and will announce future schedules at a later date."
The testing period was meant to last until around 5pm BST, approximately three hours from now. There are still testing periods scheduled throughout the weekend into Monday, so here's hoping the server issue gets fixed soon.
Hey, this is a network test after all - isn't dealing with these problems part of what it's all about?
ORIGINAL STORY 12PM BST: The Duskbloods closed network test has begun, offering players an early peek at FromSoftware's upcoming PvPvE action game ahead of launch later this year. And with reports of connectivity issues already coming in, FromSoftware has offered some somewhat old-fashioned advice for dealing with it.
On social media, testers report finding themselves stuck on the title screen, unable to actually enter a match. These players appear to be getting stuck while attempting to connect to The Duskbloods servers, suggesting a wider issue.
Here's where FromSoftware stepped in with an official post on the game's X account, which offered the following advice: "If using a wireless internet connection while playing The Duskbloods Closed Network Test, you may experience instability depending on your network environment. In this case, please try connecting while near your router/modem, or switching to a wired connection."
If that doesn't work, an official post on The Duskbloods website urged players to refer to the Nintendo Support website. This page is a basic FAQ about online services on Switch 2.
This - as you have likely assumed doesn't seem to have solved the problem for those affected by server connectivity issues. Still, there's plenty of time left in the game's testing period, which runs until Monday. Here's hoping this problem is resolved soon, and players get to check out the game firsthand. With, or without, sitting next to their router.
summary: FromSoftware ended the first day of The Duskbloods network test early due to persistent connectivity and game server issues. Players had reported getting stuck on the title screen and being unable to enter matches. The company apologized for the inconvenience and stated they will announce future testing schedules after working on server improvements.
key_points: FromSoftware closed the first day of The Duskbloods network test ahead of schedule.
Players experienced server issues and got stuck on the title screen unable to join matches.
The company suggested using a wired connection or moving closer to the router to address instability.
Additional testing periods remain scheduled throughout the weekend and into Monday.

title: Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 Is Getting Great Reviews Ahead Of Release
author: Pure Xbox; Fraser Gilbert
content:
![Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 Is Getting Great Reviews Ahead Of Release](https://images.purexbox.com/6b45c8d8a3abf/metal-gear-solid-master-collection-vol-2-is-getting-great-reviews-ahead-of-release.900x.jpg)
Next week marks the arrival of Metal Gear Solid 4 on Xbox for the very first time as part of the new Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol.2, and that collection is unsurprisingly getting some great review scores ahead of release.
The collection also includes Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker (the HD Collection version), and you can choose to buy each of these games separately if you'd prefer. Buying the collection grants you access to a few extra goodies though, including the first ever handheld MGS game in the form of Metal Gear: Ghost Babel from 2000.
So, here's what the reviews are saying about this one (although keep in mind they're all based on the PS5 version, as Xbox codes don't seem to have been widely circulated yet):
VGC (5/5)
"It's hard to think of a better collection of games than those on Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2. Even if Metal Gear Solid 4 wasn't such a prize for players who haven't been able to revisit it for so long, the game, divorced of that context, is still excellent. While they're less headline grabbing, Peace Walker and Ghost Babel both sit alongside the very best of the franchise. An unmissable collection for Metal Gear fans."
CGM (9/10)
"Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 brings with it two fantastic games, including one of PlayStation 3's best exclusives brought back to life like a shot of nanomachine suppressors to the leg."
Noisy Pixel (9/10)
"Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is a faithful preservation package that finally frees Metal Gear Solid 4 from the PS3 while giving Peace Walker and Ghost Babel another chance to shine. It does little to modernize the games beyond making them accessible, but strong ports, worthwhile extras, and the enduring quality of the originals make this an easy recommendation for longtime fans."
COGConnected (8.5/10)
"Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 features some of the best games in the series. MGS 4 is without doubt a masterpiece, and this port improves on the original by adding a locked frame rate. While Peace Walker is the same as the previous port, it’s still a brilliant game that offers a co-operative spin on the formula. The GBC adventure tops off the package, highlighting the diversity of experiences that have defined the franchise."
Push Square (8/10)
"After nearly twenty years chained to the proverbial radiator that is the PlayStation 3, Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots finally arrives on PS5. The nanomachines, the fashion model robot monsters, the flamenco dance battle, the fried eggs, the cigarette smoking underpants monkey, and that ridiculous final boss, all running at 60 frames-per-second and looking better than ever. This is good, isn't it?"
summary: Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is receiving positive review scores ahead of its upcoming release. The collection notably brings Metal Gear Solid 4 to Xbox for the first time and frees it from the PlayStation 3, alongside Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker and Metal Gear: Ghost Babel. Reviewers praise the enduring quality of the titles and the addition of features like a locked frame rate, though current reviews are primarily based on the PlayStation 5 version.
key_points: Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 includes Metal Gear Solid 4, Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker, and Metal Gear: Ghost Babel.
The collection marks the first time Metal Gear Solid 4 is available on Xbox.
Games can be purchased as a collection or separately.
Early reviews for the collection are generally positive, highlighting strong ports and the preservation of classic titles.

title: The ‘GTA 6’ Leaker Is Leaking Again, Ending Rumors Of Being Caught
author: Paul Tassi
content:
After the usually chatty Grand Theft Auto 6 leaker went a full 24 hours without posting anything, many began to theorize Cyberleek’s spree was over, and they’d been shut down or caught after Take-Two’s relentless pursuit. That does not appear to be the case.
This morning, a new leak called “Hypercar” was uploaded to Cyberleek’s website. Given that it was within the past hour, it’s been hard to find, but I did locate the full 2:25 video before it was taken down. There will soon be a lot of these spread around and shot down by Take-Two as has happened with every GTA 6 leak so far. But it’s been impossible to stop the flow.
The new footage shows Jason smashing the window on a Bugatti-like car, the Truffade Thrax, and pulling the driver out. A typical GTA action, but this GTA 6 one looks a little more involved, as you also have to tap a button to drag the driver from the car.
The rest of the leak is the car driving around the city, at one point ironically stopping at a stop sign. After this, it’s just about two minutes of uneventful driving. No crashes, no hitting pedestrians. The footage is stamped with the usual crypto coin ad to funnel money to Cyberleek, but this time also a “Cyberleek can’t drive” message, possibly referring to some making fun of them in past clips for not playing the game terribly well.
![frase](https://images.forbes.com/fbs-games-assets/frase.png)
FEATURED | Frase ByForbes™
Unscramble The Anagram To Reveal The Phrase
![pinpoint](https://images.forbes.com/fbs-games-assets/pinpoint.png)
Pinpoint By Linkedin
Guess The Category
![queens](https://images.forbes.com/fbs-games-assets/queens.png)
Queens By Linkedin
Crown Each Region
![crossclimb](https://images.forbes.com/fbs-games-assets/crossclimb.png)
Crossclimb By Linkedin
Unlock A Trivia Ladder
This is the sixth major leak from Cyberleek, the last of which seemed to confirm the leaker has an actual build of the game rather than just taking gameplay clips from somewhere. He wrote “LEEKS” on the wall with bullets, indicating live gameplay of what appears to be a build from 2025. The 24 hour silence did lead many to believe his joyride was over, and he must have been discovered. This new leak would indicate that is not the case.
Despite how high-profile this series of leaks has been, and how it is a nightmare scenario for Rockstar that this person has an actual playable build of the game, nothing all that damaging has actually been released. It’s just been typical GTA stuff like fighting random NPCs, stealing cars, flying a plane, shooting a gun. Even the cutscene snippet shown revealed nothing, and was just a brief jab at Rockstar about someone using a VPN.
Of course, there is always the risk that Cyberleek could start veering into actual story spoilers, which would be exceptionally damaging. While it does seem likely that they will be stopped or caught at some point, we’re pushing toward a week and it hasn’t happened yet. Outside of this, other leaks from other places in other formats are starting to trickle out as well. Nothing this big, but with three months to go, it’s easy to see how this is going to quickly become a game of whack-a-mole with a Rockstar that is not as secure as it needs to be, clearly.
I’ve been reaching out to Rockstar and will update if I hear back. It has not yet issued a public statement on these leaks.
Follow me on Twitter, YouTube, and Instagram.
Pick up my sci-fi novels the Herokiller series and The Earthborn Trilogy.
summary: Rumors that the "GTA 6" leaker Cyberleek had been caught were disproven after a new gameplay video titled "Hypercar" was uploaded. The footage shows a character breaking into a Truffade Thrax and driving around the city. This marks the sixth major leak from Cyberleek, who appears to possess an actual playable build of the game.
key_points: A 24-hour silence from Cyberleek sparked rumors that the leaker had been caught.
A new 2:25 video leak called "Hypercar" was uploaded to Cyberleek's website before being taken down.
The footage shows a character smashing a car window, dragging the driver out, and driving through the city.
This is the sixth major leak from Cyberleek, indicating the leaker has an actual playable build of the game.
Rockstar has not yet issued a public statement regarding the ongoing leaks.

title: This app does with Pixel 11 Pro's HiLight what Google should have done in the first place
author: Aamir Siddiqui
content:
This app does with Pixel 11 Pro's HiLight what Google should have done in the first place
Aug 20, 2026 — 5:53 AM ET
![Pixel 11 HiLight Studio Rainbow 3 Pixel 11 HiLight Studio Rainbow 3](https://www.androidauthority.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Pixel-11-HiLight-Studio-Rainbow-3-scaled.jpg)
- Google heavily restricted the Pixel 11 Pro’s rear HiLight LED array out of the box, limiting it to Gemini and calls from favorite contacts.
- The open-source HiLight Studio app unlocks the LED’s full potential with custom app notifications, light patterns (comet, pulse, rainbow), Quick Settings toggles, and built-in hardware protection limits.
- You can set up the app by sideloading its APK and granting core permissions using Shizuku over Wireless debugging.
The Pixel 11 Pro series has a new “HiLight” LED system built around the camera’s flash on the back of the device. HiLight can be used as a notification LED to let you know about calls from your favorite contacts, and it also glows when you’re having a Gemini conversation… and that’s about it. HiLight has plenty of potential, but disappointingly, Google hasn’t blessed it with much functionality out of the box. If you want more out of HiLight and are okay with taking matters into your own hands, the open-source HiLight Studio app supercharges Pixel 11 Pro’s HiLight LED so it’s actually useful.
HiLight Studio is an open-source app by YouTuber-turned-vibecoder Dhananjay Bhosale that expands HiLight’s functionality beyond just favorite calls and Gemini, allowing you to configure the notification LED to work with any app you choose. The HiLight LED can be activated either when the app sends you a notification, when it’s open, or both if you want. You can set any color for any app, or even go crazier with multiple pattern options like comet, pulse, breathe, wave, or even rainbow.
If you can’t decide which option to choose, HiLight Studio also lets you save presets and import or export them for backup and sharing. Further, you can also pull in colors from your wallpaper if you’re gunning for a cohesive look for your phone.
Beyond customization, HiLight Studio also gives you full, easy control over all its HiLight functionality. It comes with a Quick Settings tile that lets you toggle its features on and off without opening the app. It also respects your Do Not Disturb settings, and you can also set quiet hours separately. HiLight Studio also pauses its functionality when your battery drops below the level you set.
All of this control is great, but the HiLight LED array wasn’t designed to stay on continuously for long stretches, so HiLight Studio complements it with built-in safety limits. The developer notes that the LED array’s brightness will be gradually dimmed automatically if it remains on for more than 10 seconds at a time. If you’ve set the LED to turn on when an app opens, it will automatically switch off after 30 seconds by default, though you can extend this to a maximum of five minutes after clicking through a few warnings. Notification colors are capped to a minute maximum.
There’s also a global safety limit: the LED will not remain active for more than 5 minutes within any 10-minute period, regardless of your configuration. Whenever any of these safety precautions are triggered, the app also informs you about it.
While the app is vibe-coded with AI, it has been tested extensively on the developer’s Pixel 11 Pro XL. The developer also assures us that the app will remain open-source, ad-free, and subscription-free.
How to set up and use HiLight Studio on your Pixel 11 Pro/Pro XL/Pro Fold to control HiLight
You can download HiLight Studio from GitHub and install it on your Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, or Pixel 11 Pro Fold like any sideloadable APK. However, you’ll need Shizuku to activate the app’s core functionality after every reboot:
- Install Shizuku from the Play Store.
- Open Shizuku and start it via Wireless debugging. Shizuku will walk you through the pairing process.
- Once Shizuku is installed, open HiLight Studio > Setup > Request access, then allow access when Shizuku prompts you for it.
Once you have the core functionality set up, you have to grant HiLight Studio “Notification access” when you want notification rules, and “Usage access” when you want a rule to run while an app is open. The app’s Setup tab guides you through all of this. There’s an ADB-driven setup too, but we couldn’t get the command to work on our end.
Our experience with HiLight Studio on a Pixel 11 Pro XL
![HiLight Studio Rainbow color 2 HiLight Studio Rainbow color 2](https://www.androidauthority.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/HiLight-Studio-Rainbow-color-2.jpg)
My colleague Adamya Sharma tried out HiLight Studio on her Pixel 11 Pro XL. For her, installing the app was probably the trickiest part of the whole experience. The ADB method didn’t work for her, and getting Shizuku set up and granting it the necessary permissions took some effort. She also had to navigate Android’s Play Protect warnings and other restrictions before she could actually get the app running.
Once she got past all of that, though, the app worked pretty well for what it promises. You get six different effects — Rainbow, Random, Comet, Pulse, Breathe, and Wave — and you can assign different colors to individual apps. One of the coolest features is the ability to create your own color presets for the LEDs.
You can even customize each LED color individually, so you can pick up to 10 different colors and adjust their saturation, intensity, and brightness to create your own patterns.
![HiLight Studio 1 HiLight Studio 1](https://www.androidauthority.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/HiLight-Studio-1-scaled.jpg)
You can also set up rules for individual apps and decide exactly how HiLight should react when you receive notifications from them. By default, HiLight turns off after 30 seconds, but you can extend that to five minutes with a toggle. There are also options to keep it disabled at certain times, which is particularly useful if you don’t want your phone lighting up in the middle of the night.
Overall, she found the app to be pretty cool. It’s the kind of feature that makes you wonder why Google didn’t offer something like this itself. Perhaps there are technical reasons for keeping tighter control over the LEDs, such as concerns about their longevity, but HiLight shows just how much more flexibility Google could have offered from the start. That’s something a lot of users have been unhappy about.
![Pixel 11 HiLight Studio 4 Pixel 11 HiLight Studio 4](https://www.androidauthority.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Pixel-11-HiLight-Studio-4.jpg)
There is one pretty big caveat with her experience, though. After installing and using HiLight, the base feature stopped working properly on her phone. She was no longer seeing the LEDs light up when talking to Gemini or when receiving calls from my favorite contacts, two situations where HiLight is actually supposed to work.
She deleted the app and restarted her Pixel 11 Pro XL, and everything went back to normal. So while the app does a pretty good job of unlocking more control over the LEDs, in her case, it also seemed to interfere with some of the system’s built-in HiLight functionality. For now, she’ll be sticking with Google’s implementation.
summary: Google severely restricts the Pixel 11 Pro's rear HiLight LED array out of the box, limiting its use to Gemini and favorite contact calls. To address this, an open-source app called HiLight Studio unlocks the hardware for custom app notifications, patterns, and color presets. However, testing revealed that the app can sometimes interfere with the phone's native built-in HiLight functionality until it is uninstalled.
key_points: Google limits the Pixel 11 Pro's HiLight LED array to Gemini conversations and favorite contact calls.
The open-source HiLight Studio app allows users to configure custom app notifications, light patterns, and color presets.
The app includes hardware protection limits to prevent the LEDs from overheating or degrading over time.
Setting up HiLight Studio requires sideloading the APK and using Shizuku via Wireless debugging for permissions.
One test user found that the app successfully added custom features but temporarily disabled native Pixel HiLight functions until removed.
